title: Brent Flirts With $110 Before Reversing As Wright Declares Pump Prices Have "Peaked"
desc:
Brent Flirts With $110 Before Reversing As Wright Declares Pump Prices Have "Peaked"

Brent crude futures briefly tagged $109.99 a barrel in overnight trading before retreating from five-month highs during the Asian session and into European trading, as signs of recovering Middle Eastern supply offset renewed attacks on energy infrastructure and critical maritime shipping lanes.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright reinforced expectations of easing fuel prices at the pump, with ABC News quoting him on Sunday as saying gasoline and diesel prices had "peaked."

"Both gasoline and diesel prices peaked a few weeks ago," Wright said, adding that the US wants them to "pull back a lot more than they have."

He said he understands the mounting frustrations at the pump, which have soured consumer sentiment, but said the administration is "working in all different avenues" to address the problem.

The latest data from AAA show the national average for diesel prices at the pump on Sunday stood at around $6.319 a gallon, down from the previous record high of $6.50.

AAA pump data also show regular gasoline prices sliding from the $4.50 level to $4.295 by Sunday, still above the politically sensitive $4 level.

Wright said Gulf oil flows had recovered to about 80% of pre-conflict levels, although refined-product shipments remained heavily constrained amid a global refining crisis compounded by Ukraine's persistent attacks on Russian refineries.

Separately, Wright told Fox News that Trump administration officials were discussing releases of diesel stockpiles in coordination with European allies.

June Goh, a senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities SA, told Bloomberg, "The markets seem unwilling to absorb the higher prices with the rest of the economy not looking rosy," adding that Brent crude is likely to remain around $100.

The Wall Street Journal reported overnight that Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed talks next month with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Moscow confirmed discussions were underway.

Last week, the International Energy Agency reinforced Goldman Sachs energy analyst Nikhil Bhandari's warning that there is no quick relief at the pump, as the refining crisis, particularly in diesel, will persist well into next year.

In another episode of the "death of Europe," a new report from Germany brings more troubling news for struggling automaker Volkswagen, suggesting to us that globalists in the bloc have squandered not just their inheritance but their economic future through a failing progressive experiment that has neutered Europe's industrial base.

German daily newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) reports that Volkswagen plans to freeze salaries through the end of the decade as it expands its cost-cutting push after lowering its outlook and doubling its job-reduction target.

"Internal documents reveal that hundreds of thousands of employees are to forgo pay raises. These latest plans represent a further escalation in the conflict between management and employee representatives," SZ wrote in the article.

title: Europe Braces For A Winter Energy Crisis As Gas Reserves Run Low
desc:
Europe Braces For A Winter Energy Crisis As Gas Reserves Run Low

Authored by Felicity Bradstock via OilPrice,

  • Europe faces another expensive winter as low gas reserves and Middle East disruptions drive up energy prices.

  • Rising fuel costs threaten household budgets, industrial production, and employment across Europe.

  • Increased U.S. LNG supplies could provide some relief, but continued geopolitical risks leave energy markets vulnerable.

After months of elevated energy prices, Europe can expect fuel costs to continue rising through the winter months as demand grows. Ongoing energy trade constraints and threats to energy infrastructure across the Middle East are expected to limit global energy supplies and continue to drive up prices, hitting consumers hard unless governments intervene.

The European Union (EU) is thought to have paid an additional €100 billion on oil and gas so far this year, prompting EU ministers to seek ways to manage the impact of high fuel prices. Since 2022, the extra costs of energy have surpassed €900 billion, even as total demand has fallen. The price of natural gas in Europe has more than doubled since the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli-led war in Iran. This winter could be the most challenging in terms of energy supplies and prices since the start of Russia's war on Ukraine and the subsequent sanctions on Russian energy.

Meanwhile, EU energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen has warned that the winter months could be challenging amid "very high" oil and gas prices, although he reassured consumers that no supply issues are expected. Jorgensen also proposed postponing the introduction of rules to reduce methane emissions on energy imports to help ease pressure on European energy markets.

Gas storage has fallen to its lowest level since 2022. In September, across Europe, gas storage stood at around 67 per cent full, compared with a seasonal average of around 80 per cent. Germany, which has the largest storage capacity in Europe, is roughly half full, and is expected to miss its official 80 per cent storage target this year.

Meanwhile, constrained supplies due to strict limits on energy trade through the Strait of Hormuz have sharply driven up energy prices. Oil prices increased by 65 per cent, diesel by 45 per cent, and jet fuel by 112 per cent between September 25, 2025 and 2026. This has led the European Commission to call for consumers to reduce their demand throughout the year to manage supplies.

As Europe heads into its high-demand winter months, there is no end to the war in Iran in sight. In addition, the El Niño weather cycle is expected to add an element of uncertainty to weather trends, which could further complicate the gas demand picture. Threats remain to fuel shipments traversing the Strait of Hormuz, as well as ongoing threats to energy infrastructure across the Middle East. Meanwhile, Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and against pipelines continue to be a concern. Therefore, there are likely to be restrictions on global oil trade well into 2027.

The United States has focused on increasing oil and gas production to help alleviate some of the energy supply chain constraints, but this can only partly fill the gap. Atlantic and Pacific freight rates have returned to pre-Iran war levels, as a larger share of cargoes from the United States is heading to Europe rather than Asia, thereby reducing travel distances and increasing ship availability.

The independent LNG and shipping analyst Pratiksha Negi stated, "The growing share of Atlantic trade, combined with an increasing pool of prompt vessels, will continue to pressure freight rates... I expect Europe to remain the principal destination for marginal U.S. LNG at the start of Q4 2026, given the significant storage deficit this season." Negi also highlighted the rise in newbuild deliveries, with roughly 55 new vessels delivered in the first seven months of the year and another 40-45 expected by the end of the year.

Across Europe, it is not only households that are concerned about their energy bills, as several industries prepare for fuel shortages. Higher fuel prices are driving up operating costs in factories and other facilities, which could lead companies to charge more for manufactured goods, as costs will once again shift to consumers. Meanwhile, companies that cannot secure or afford adequate fuel supplies may be forced to suspend operations in the winter, leading to job cuts.

A recent forecast by the Item Club suggested that in the United Kingdom, as many as 163,000 jobs could be lost in 2026 in relation to the war, mainly in manufacturing-heavy regions such as South Wales and the Humber region. As one of Europe's biggest gas consumers, the U.K. is highly exposed to trade restrictions, particularly because it has one of the lowest levels of domestic storage capacity, which means it relies heavily on pipeline imports from Europe and tankers from the U.S. and the Middle East. The CEO of British Gas owner Centrica, Chris O'Shea, said in August that Britain had "almost no gas in storage" for the coming winter.

Both households and businesses across Europe could be hit hard this winter by the continued constraints on oil and gas supplies and high energy prices. This could force consumers to ration their consumption and may prompt the European Commission and governments to intervene to ensure consumers have access to vital energy supplies.

title: 70% Of Moroccan Asylee Claims In Ceuta After Mass Entry Cite Persecution Over Sexual Orientation
desc:
70% Of Moroccan Asylee Claims In Ceuta After Mass Entry Cite Persecution Over Sexual Orientation

Spanish police say about 70% of the Moroccans processed in Ceuta after July's mass entry have asked for asylum alleging persecution over their sexual orientation, according to El Periódico de Ceuta, which relays figures from National Police sources first published by the Spanish daily ABC. The number comes from unnamed police sources, not published statistics.

The paper says officers handling migration in the enclave see a shift from the economic or work reasons Moroccans usually gave, and that the claims have reshaped the caseload at the city's asylum office. Morocco-focused outlet Yabiladi reports that the sources suspect some applicants are being coached on asylum procedures as a way to stay in Spain.

Only five of those who arrived in the mass entries have so far won refugee status for persecution over homosexuality, El Periódico says. Spain's Office of Asylum and Refugees reviews each file individually, and the paper says investigators are still weighing whether each account is true.

Being gay is not enough by itself, Yabiladi notes: applicants must show a well-founded risk of persecution if sent back, judged on interviews, consistency, documents and conditions in Morocco, and without relying on stereotypes. Morocco criminalizes same-sex relations under Article 489 of its penal code, and the U.S. State Department says hundreds of men and women are prosecuted for it each year, per AP.

Neither report says how many claims sit behind the 70% figure. El Periódico describes it as a share of Moroccans attended after the entries, while Yabiladi calls it 70% of applications, so the denominator is unclear.

Some claimants have told their stories. An AP report on Oct. 11 quoted a gay man from Tetouan who left after his brother threatened to report him to police: "I left Morocco because being gay is so hard." AP said it could not independently verify the asylum claim of one interviewee. Police cleared the beachside tent camp in early October.

The scale of the July 30-31 entry is itself disputed. Spanish government estimates put the number who reached the city at 72,000, many swimming around the border fence, the Irish Times reported in August. The government counted 83 deaths and a human rights group 141. Most of those who crossed were sent back to Morocco, several thousand remain, and Yabiladi puts the number still in the city at about 10,000.

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska has said none of the migrants will stay in Ceuta or travel to the mainland. Spain raised police and Civil Guard numbers in the city from 1,100 to 1,600, and Morocco put soldiers and extra fencing along the border. Madrid blamed traffickers, but the cause of the crossing has not been identified.

title: Germany's Rent Control Is Backfiring, New Study Of 107 Cities Finds
desc:
Germany's Rent Control Is Backfiring, New Study Of 107 Cities Finds

Authored by Rainer Zitelmann via RealClearMarkets,

Across Europe, the housing shortage is getting worse - and left-wing parties have discovered it as a central political issue. Recently, the far-left party DIE LINKE even won the elections in Berlin, the German capital, campaigning on a demand to nationalize large housing companies. In Spain, hundreds of thousands of people have demonstrated in favor of stricter regulations.

But do such measures really help?

We should learn from Germany's experience, where a form of rent control known as the "Mietpreisbremse" (rent brake) was introduced back in 2015 and has since been tightened several times.

Yet this rent control policy is producing precisely the opposite of what it was intended to achieve. That is the conclusion of a new doctoral dissertation completed at the University of Regensburg, Europe's leading university for real estate studies.

In Germany, the gap between rents paid by existing tenants and rents charged for newly rented apartments is growing wider. In his 2026 dissertation, "Housing Markets Between Regional Heterogeneity and Political Intervention," Lars Jagemann analyzes 107 German cities. He finds that the gap between existing rents and asking rents for new leases averages 20 to 25 percent, reaching as much as 50 percent in major metropolitan areas.

This creates what economists call a "lock-in effect." As Jagemann explains, existing tenants hold on to their inexpensive, legally protected rental contracts and avoid moving into the more expensive segment of the market, even when their current homes no longer suit their circumstances.

As a result, the supply of housing available to people who need to move, such as young families or those starting their careers, shrinks, making it increasingly difficult for them to find an apartment. The market becomes increasingly divided into two groups: "insiders," who benefit from stable, inexpensive rental contracts protected by regulation, and "outsiders," who are looking for housing and face sharply rising market rents for new leases.

The dissertation confirms what economists have repeatedly warned about: While German housing policy aims to promote social stability and protect tenants, the measures introduced create unintended market distortions that can, paradoxically, harm precisely those groups they are supposed to protect. Regulation, the author concludes, is becoming increasingly "dysfunctional."

In theory, there are two possible responses: even more regulation, or deregulation and greater reliance on market forces. The author himself makes no direct recommendation. It would have been desirable for the dissertation to examine in greater detail the problems associated with even stricter regulation, particularly the "interventionist spiral" identified by economist Ludwig von Mises.

According to Mises, tighter regulations may temporarily alleviate certain problems, but they create new ones. Governments then introduce additional regulations to address these problems, which in turn produce further unintended consequences.

In fact, the dissertation provides empirical confirmation of this mechanism. Since Germany introduced its rent brake in 2015, the policy has already been tightened several times. The so-called "Kappungsgrenze," which limits rent increases for existing tenants, has also been made more restrictive.

The central finding of the dissertation is that precisely because housing is a fundamental social need, housing policy interventions must respect the inherent mechanisms of the market. Regulations that work against fundamental economic incentives provoke avoidance strategies that can place additional burdens on vulnerable groups. Sustainable housing policy, so the authors, must therefore make intelligent use of market mechanisms rather than fight them: by creating incentives instead of imposing prohibitions, expanding supply instead of capping prices, and establishing transparent, long-term rules instead of constantly changing interventions.

The author also places particular emphasis on the damaging effects of political uncertainty. Such uncertainty is created not only by actual government policies. Even the discussion of possible new regulations can generate uncertainty, prompting investors to adopt a wait-and-see approach.

Uncertainty is always bad for investors, but it is particularly damaging in real estate, the author argues, because investments require long planning periods and are largely irreversible. Unlike stocks, investors cannot simply exit a construction project at any time without losing substantial amounts of money.

Here, too, a vicious circle develops: uncertainty reduces housing supply, which drives up property prices and rents. These increases are then used to justify new political demands for intervention, creating even more uncertainty.

Alongside healthcare and finance, housing is among the most heavily regulated markets in many countries. It is no coincidence that these are precisely the sectors that experience recurring crises. More regulation increases costs and reduces efficiency.

Across Europe, center-right parties are making the mistake of leaving housing policy to the left instead of making problems such as high rents and housing shortages central issues themselves. They should demonstrate that only sweeping deregulation can substantially expand housing supply. Javier Milei is currently showing exactly how this can be done in Argentina.BIO: In June, Skyhorse Publishing will release Rainer Zitelmann's book "New Space Capitalism."

title: 80% Of New UK Payroll Jobs Since 2014 Went To Foreign Nationals, Think Tank Finds
desc:
80% Of New UK Payroll Jobs Since 2014 Went To Foreign Nationals, Think Tank Finds

Just one in five of the roughly 3.7 million jobs added to UK payrolls from 2014 through the end of 2025 went to British nationals. Non-EU nationals took about 2.5 million of them, roughly two-thirds, and EU nationals another 408,000, leaving Britons with 734,000, according to a Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) analysis of HMRC data.

The center-right think tank released the figures Tuesday in State of Dependency, a 250-page report launching its Welfare 2030 inquiry. Former Work and Pensions Secretary Sir Iain Duncan Smith chairs the inquiry.

The CSJ's rounded components add to about 3.64 million against its "approximately 3.7 million" total, so foreign nationals took close to 80% of the growth and Britons about 20%. Britons still hold most of the jobs that exist: HMRC data show 25.6 million Britons among 32 million payrolled workers in December 2025, the Press Association reported.

The shift is recent. Since January 2020, Britons' payroll jobs fell in nine of the UK's 12 regions and nations while non-EU nationals' jobs rose in all 12, the CSJ's regional table shows. Summed across that table, non-EU nationals gained about 2.1 million payroll jobs, Britons lost about 186,000 and EU nationals lost about 352,000. More than four-fifths of the non-EU gain since 2014 therefore came in the last six years of the twelve.

London shows it most sharply. Non-EU payroll jobs there rose by 465,200 since 2020 while Britons' fell by 26,500 and EU nationals' by 171,100. Scotland lost 53,000 British payroll jobs and gained 130,200 non-EU ones; the South East lost 31,700 and gained 284,500. Four sectors account for about two-thirds of the non-EU increase: health and social work (29%), administrative and support services (16%), accommodation and food (12%), and wholesale and retail (10%).

Care shows how the door opened. In the year to March 2023, about 57,700 care and senior care workers received skilled-worker visas, and 99% of sponsored care workers in 2022 came from outside the EU, according to the Migration Observatory. Inflows have since fallen: the ONS put net migration at 171,000 in 2025, from 331,000 a year earlier, with work-related arrivals of non-EU nationals down 47% to about 146,000 after rule changes that included closing the Health and Care route for overseas care workers. The CSJ's payroll window ends in December 2025, so it captures the hiring wave and only part of the 2024 and 2025 restrictions.

The other half of the CSJ's case is welfare. It counts 6.7 million people on at least one out-of-work benefit, about one in six working-age adults, and says out-of-work claimants rose by 2.3 million between February 2020 and November 2025. Working-age benefits are forecast to cost £136.1 billion in 2026/27, up about £50 billion in real terms since 2019/20, and the report identifies 3,369 "welfare hotspots" where claimants outnumber half the working-age population, home to nearly 900,000 people.

A companion CSJ estimate puts the foreign-national share at about 1.85 million non-British adults receiving at least one benefit or the state pension in 2025, at roughly £23 billion, including 1.3 million on Universal Credit at £11.9 billion. Those are CSJ calculations from DWP, HMRC and Home Office data and survey rates, not official statistics, and they assume half the adults in mixed-nationality households are foreign nationals. Earlier estimates ran lower: as we reported, one analysis of government data put welfare paid to migrants at £7.6 billion in a single year.

The report's thesis is that governments swapped one dependency for another. Real GDP grew 26% from 2006 to 2025, but real GDP per person grew only 10%, which the CSJ calls "human quantitative easing": importing workers to lift headline growth. It adds that official fiscal forecasts run only five years, so they bank the early tax take from migrant workers and miss the welfare costs that arrive later. Duncan Smith said "ministers have repeatedly pulled the easy lever of immigration rather than providing a better deal for left behind communities."

He has made the jobs argument before. As work and pensions secretary in July 2011, Duncan Smith told a Madrid audience that businesses should hire unemployed Britons, and Channel 4 noted that 87% of the 400,000 jobs created in the coalition's first year had gone to workers from abroad, a figure unearthed by Labour MP Frank Field. The same caution applies here. The CSJ counts net changes in payrolled jobs by nationality, not who was hired, and a naturalized citizen counts as British. In 2015 the Daily Express claimed 75% of new jobs went to EU migrants; the paper corrected it after economist Jonathan Portes complained and the press regulator IPSO ruled it "significantly misleading," because the ONS data showed net changes in employment, not people entering new jobs.

The report landed a day after Reform UK's Nigel Farage pledged to suspend the asylum system for a full parliament, as we reported.

title: Dutch Minister: Young Locals Can Just Live With Their Parents, Migrants Get Houses First
desc:
Dutch Minister: Young Locals Can Just Live With Their Parents, Migrants Get Houses First

Via Remix News,

Dutch Housing Minister Elanor Boekholt-O'Sullivan drew sharp criticism this week after defending priority access to scarce social housing for recognized refugees, arguing that many young Dutch first-time home seekers "can still live with their parents."

In an interview with De Telegraaf, the D66 minister was asked why status holders - asylum seekers granted residence permits - should receive preference for social rental homes while Dutch "starters" face long waiting lists and delayed independence. She responded that "we see that a lot of starters can still, or are allowed to, live with their parents."

?? Migrants get affordable housing before Dutch natives. When asked why migrants receive access to affordable housing before young Dutch people looking for a "starter" home, the Dutch housing minister said that many Dutch first-time home seekers "can still live with their parents." Mass migration contributed to 60% of the increase in housing demand in the Netherlands since 2015, yet Minister Elanor Boekholt-O'Sullivan still believes in putting migrants first. "For me, the fundamental principle is that anyone who is allowed to and wants to live in the Netherlands gets a roof over their head," she said. In the Netherlands, Dutch natives are increasingly relegated to living with their parents while migrants get to skip massive waiting lists and gain "emergency" access to cheap social housing. Follow: @RMXnews

— Remix News & Views (@RMXnews) October 14, 2026

Dutch commentator and activist Eva Vlaardingerbroek wrote on X that the policy amounted to "systemic racism."

"And not just the 'new' newcomers. A 25-year-old Syrian who came here with his parents years ago jumps the queue for a home when he decides he wants to live on his own. Meaning a 25-year-old white Dutch guy can forget about getting his own place and ends up on waiting lists for 10+ years," she wrote, adding: "Putting the interests of foreigners above the interests of the native population needs to end."

Talking about systemic racism: Young Dutch people can barely find a place to live, because migration drove 60% of the housing demand since 2015, regular prices are insane, and migrants get PRIORITY for the affordable social housing. And not just the "new" newcomers. A 25-year-old Syrian who came here with his parents years ago jumps the queue for a home when he decides he wants to live on his own. Meaning a 25 year-old white Dutch guy can forget about getting his own place and ends up on waiting lists for 10+ years. But according to our minister of housing that's fine because they can just continue to "live with their parents." Putting the interests of foreigners above the interests of the native population, needs to end. That's why with the @SaveEuropeAct, apart from demanding closed borders and Remigration, we also demand ?Removing social welfare incentives and benefits that function as pull factors for migration.

— Eva Vlaardingerbroek (@EvaVlaar) October 13, 2026

Boekholt-O'Sullivan, an Irish-born former lieutenant general in the Dutch Air Force who took office earlier this year, claims that anyone who wants to live in the Netherlands should get a roof but does not address the major housing crisis brought on by mass immigration.

"For me, the fundamental principle is that anyone who is allowed to and wants to live in the Netherlands gets a roof over their head," she said. She noted that status holders typically leave asylum reception centers and argued that alternatives such as remaining in centers, homelessness, hotels or cruise ships were unacceptable, so priority allocation should continue until other solutions exist.

The remarks landed amid fresh data underscoring migration's outsized role in the Netherlands' housing crunch. A report released this week by the Economic Institute for Construction (EIB) found that migration accounted for about 60 percent of additional housing demand between 2015 and 2024. Migrants who arrived in that period occupied roughly 435,000 homes by 2024, out of nearly 700,000 homes added to the stock.

In addition, data shows that migrants occupy 44 percent of the 2.2 million social housing units in the country.

The 44 percent figure of social housing units occupied by first or second-generation immigrants has doubled from 22 percent in 2000, and is forecast to rise to 51 percent by 2030.

A total of 92 percent of Syrian first-generation immigrants reside in social housing. In addition, 90 percent of those born in Somalia, Afghanistan, and Eritrea reside in social housing.

Asylum-related migration contributes disproportionately to lasting demand because status holders remain permanently at high rates, unlike many labor or student migrants who leave within a decade.

Critics said the minister's comments minimized the burdens on young Dutch adults who have already spent years on waiting lists for social housing or who face high private rents and purchase prices that lock them out of independent living.

Social housing waiting lists in major cities often stretch many years; priority rules for status holders allow some recent arrivals to bypass ordinary queues. Dutch population growth in recent years has been driven almost entirely by net migration, amplifying pressure on an already constrained housing market marked by strict planning rules, nitrogen regulations and slow construction.

The latest debate about Dutch housing policy and mass immigration is only one aspect of the massive burden foreigners have been on Dutch society, which shows that Dutch taxpayers have spent €400 billion on migrants between 1995 and 2019.

The landmark study, entitled "Borderless Welfare State: The Consequences of Immigration on Public Finances," shows that net costs of immigration to the Dutch public sector over the period 1995-2019 were an astounding €400 billion, averaging €17 billion a year, with a peak of €32 billion in 2016 due to the 2015 refugee crisis.

However, this is far from the total figure. Since 2019, Dutch taxpayers have paid tens of billions more, with no end in sight.

title: Omar, Obama, And The Danger Of False Identities
desc:
Omar, Obama, And The Danger Of False Identities

Authored by J.B. Shurk via American Thinker,

On Columbus Day, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant of Representative Ilhan Omar's home. For several months, there have been rumors that she was under investigation for immigration fraud. A few weeks ago, White House Border Czar Tom Homan acknowledged that the congresswoman was the subject of an ongoing criminal investigation. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro says her office is investigating Omar for potential financial crimes. The D.C. magistrate judge who authorized the search of Omar's residence is a registered Democrat who donated to Hillary Clinton and received professional appointments from other Democrats.

Despite the fact that Democrats wholeheartedly cheered when President Joe Biden and Attorney General Merrick Garland authorized FBI agents to use deadly force against the Trump family when they raided his Mar-a-Lago home in 2022 to retrieve evidence of the Department of Justice's unlawful spying operations against Republican politicians during Barack Obama's presidency, the people who repeatedly told us for years that "nobody is above the law" now insist that the raid of Omar's residence is an "abuse of power," "political retribution," and the act of "a fascist police state."

As news of the Omar raid broke, CNN's Jake Tapper called it "vindictive" and questioned whether it was a "legitimate law enforcement action." Tapper's supposedly expert guest - a Democrat lawfare operative - responded to the host's predetermined judgment of the investigation by calling it, "Partisan. Racism. Xenophobia."

Bill Kristol - who, amazingly enough, was once regarded as a trusted public intellectual among Republican voters before revealing himself to have been a complete fraud who lied about almost everything he long claimed to believe - posted this urgent request on X: "Now is the time for all good men to come to the aid of their country." When FBI agents were pawing through First Lady Melania Trump's undergarments back in 2022, Kristol encouraged Americans to be patient and to avoid any rush to judgment - even though the criminal targeting of an American president was unprecedented and shocking.

MS NOW's "Justice and Intel Reporter," Ken Dilanian pointed out that most immigrants' naturalization paperwork contains "fudged facts" - essentially arguing that since many foreigners lie to authorities, Omar shouldn't be singled out and prosecuted for committing immigration fraud. This is a rather unjust double standard for a "justice" reporter to articulate given that Americans who "fudge facts" on legal documents are regularly prosecuted for the crimes of misrepresentation, forgery, and fraud.

Unless and until Representative Omar is actually indicted, the public will have to wait to read about the particular facts of her case. It is worth noting, however, that numerous allegations have swirled around the congresswoman for years. Several of her Democrat primary opponents alleged that she had committed immigration fraud on behalf of herself and other members of her family. Public investigations suggest that she falsified her birthdate in order to obtain naturalized citizenship. There have been reports that she married her biological brother as part of a fraudulent scheme to provide him American citizenship. A number of historians claim that Omar's father "misrepresented himself as a refugee" and was instead a military commander in a Somali dictatorship responsible for several hundred thousand murders. The congresswoman insists that her birth records were destroyed during Somalia's civil war (a bloody conflict during which her father may have committed crimes against humanity).

Perhaps we will learn whether these allegations have merit in the months ahead. What I do know is that this inquiry is long overdue. The appearance of impropriety has followed Representative Omar even before she joined Congress in 2019. Allegations of immigration fraud have been loud - including the unsavory claim that she married her brother - yet neither congressional leaders nor federal officials have been inclined to investigate the matter more fully until now. The lack of curiosity and continued silence from authorities have been impossible for the American people to ignore.

Two-tiered justice in the United States has been with us for quite some time. Democrat lawfare drove President Nixon from the White House. President Bill Clinton targeted Christians and gun-owners and reoriented intelligence agencies away from communist organizations that were monitored during the Cold War and toward "right-wing" groups that had never posed a national security threat.

When President Obama took the reins of the federal government, he combined Clinton's targeting of conservatives with President Bush's new domestic surveillance system authorized by the USA PATRIOT Act and maliciously - yet ironically - redefined American patriots as "potential domestic terrorists." Over the course of the Obama and Biden presidencies, Christians, conservatives, libertarians, and Republican voters have been investigated for imaginary "crimes" at the behest of Democrat partisans within the federal government.

When a woman from Somalia can come to the United States and join Congress with less scrutiny than a random American Christian receives for praying outside an abortion clinic or carrying a firearm, the entire government - especially the criminal justice system - loses credibility, if not legitimacy.

Congresswoman Omar is certainly not the first member of the federal government to have been accused of committing identity fraud. Although the corporate "news" oligarchy and the political Establishment did their best to cover up the story, there were serious allegations against Barack Obama, including claims that he was not born an American citizen and was therefore ineligible to become president of the United States. As the propaganda press and the Democrat Party are doing today with regard to claims of immigration fraud against Omar, those institutions have told the American people for two decades that doubting the authenticity of Obama's Hawaiian birth certificate is an act of "racism" and "white supremacy."

However, as investigative researcher "Sundance" over at The Conservative Treehouse has long argued, there is a lot of circumstantial evidence suggesting that former CIA Director John Brennan conspired with others to scrub records from federal systems that showed Obama is not exactly who he claims to be.

Back in 2008, Brennan was an intelligence adviser to presidential candidate Obama and the CEO of an intelligence-related consulting group called The Analysis Corporation. That firm was implicated in a breach of the State Department's passport office, when one of Brennan's contract employees accessed the records of Obama, as well as those of Hillary Clinton and John McCain. Brennan's company later released this statement: "This individual's actions were taken without the knowledge or direction of anyone at The Analysis Corp. and are wholly inconsistent with our professional and ethical standards."

The State Department's inspector general later concluded that the hacker specifically sought Obama's passport file and accessed the Clinton and McCain files to create confusion for investigators. What may have been deleted from Obama's files is unknown. At the time of the incident, the Obama campaign denounced the "outrageous breach of security and privacy, even from an Administration that has shown little regard for either over the last eight years." Obama appointed Brennan director of the CIA five years later.

Obama also told reporters that any investigation "should be done in conjunction with those congressional committees that have oversight so it's not simply an internal matter." Later, State Department employee Lt. Quarles Harris, Jr. - who apparently penetrated the database and likely scrubbed Obama's records - was found dead. Harris was cooperating with investigators concerning the State Department breach at the time of his death. Barack Obama successfully hid his identity. Perhaps Ilhan Omar has John Brennan on retainer, too. We'll see.

title: "They Will All Go To Jail": Trump Threatens California Election Officials If They Let Non-Citizens Vote
desc:
"They Will All Go To Jail": Trump Threatens California Election Officials If They Let Non-Citizens Vote

On Friday President Donald Trump warned California election officials that they will go to prison if they count mail-in ballots from about 20,000 people who have been identified as possible noncitizens by the federal government, intensifying the legal dispute with the state mere weeks before the midterm elections.

California's voter registration system relies on applicants attesting to their own citizenship, and county officials argued that the system obligates them to count ballots from registered voters. The Trump administration disagrees.

"They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct. 16. He attached a copy of a Justice Department letter to Los Angeles County that promised "significant" consequences for "facilitating or ignoring" noncitizens voting in a federal election.

"The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant," the letter reads. "Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime-and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful. Under 18 U.S.C. § 611(a), noncitizens are prohibited from voting in any election involving federal offices."

The letter continued:

Under 18 U.S.C. § 2, anyone who aids, abets, counsels, induces, or procures the commission of a federal offense is equally liable. If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime. Your assertion that ballots must be counted simply because California's registration system relies on self-attestation does not relieve election officials of their obligations under federal law when they are on actual notice of noncitizen voting. Nor can state procedures supersede federal criminal statutes.

Trump's post followed a week of escalating federal action. Earlier in the week, the DOJ mailed California election officials a USB drive containing voter roll citizenship data, then sent a separate letter with the password needed to open it. According to a report from The Hill, the state had 48 hours to compare 20,000 names that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) identified as non-U.S. citizens against its own voter rolls.

On Thursday, the DOJ sued California. "If California was unable to independently confirm the citizenship of people on that list, the Federal Government asked that California set aside ballots received from them until the person's citizenship was confirmed," the lawsuit reads.

Under this approach, the state would hold the ballots in question until officials verified the voters' citizenship. The lawsuit does not ask California to discard the ballots outright.

Earlier this year, Trump said California and three other states together had 250,000 noncitizens on their voter rolls. His opponents dispute that number.

California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom called the lawsuit a "sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day."

"The courts have made clear that the federal government has no role in how a state carries out its election process, and now, in the middle of Californians voting, they have asked local officials - who do a damn good job defending democracy - to violate federal law," Newsom said, but did not specify which federal law he claims the DOJ's request would require local officials to break.

Outside groups have also moved against the administration. In September, the UCLA Voting Rights Project sued the DOJ and DHS, challenging the method the administration used to count noncitizens registered to vote. The group plans to seek a temporary restraining order if the administration does not drop its plans for a criminal crackdown on state officials.

"Your clients' actions in compiling the list violates established law; your efforts to employ this list to systematically purge voters, less than a month before the election, further violates the National Voter Registration Act, among other laws," attorneys for the group claimed in their latest letter to the DOJ.

title: Saudi Arabia At The Breaking Point
desc:
Saudi Arabia At The Breaking Point

Authored by Larry C. Johnson via Sonar 21,

For most of this war, Saudi Arabia has been the shock absorber of the world oil market. When Hormuz closed, Riyadh pushed crude west through the East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea and kept at least part of its exports moving. That bypass is now under attack. Ansar Allah has seized islands at the mouth of the Red Sea, declared a "maritime ban" on Saudi shipping and claimed strikes on Saudi airports, and in September drones knocked the East-West pipeline largely out of service. Riyadh blamed that strike on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. On October 4 a pumping station at Khurais, east of Riyadh, was hit for the first time and the pipeline stopped again.

Karl Miller, whose earlier assessment of the global fuel emergency I have drawn on before, has just completed a new analysis of what this means for Saudi Arabia and for the world. His conclusion is stark: the Gulf's energy system will take far longer and cost far more to rebuild than anyone in Washington is admitting, and Saudi Arabia can no longer be counted on to cover the gap. Here are his key findings.

1. The bypass is the weak point

Miller's starting point is that a pipeline is not a pipe. It is a connected system of pumping stations, power supplies, controls, storage tanks and loading berths, and it is only as strong as its weakest link. The September damage to the East-West pumping stations, the October interruption at Khurais, a fire at the Riyadh energy complex and the disruption of Saudi aviation all hit that system at different points. The pipeline has been partly restored, but Miller warns that permanent equipment losses remain unresolved. Yanbu can be shut down without a single bomb hitting the port: if crude stops arriving, tankers stop loading.

He also cautions against counting damaged stations as if each represented a fixed share of lost capacity. What matters is throughput, and he measures it against a benchmark of 5.8 million barrels a day through the corridor. A complete interruption for seven days would put 40.6 million barrels of movement at risk; for 30 days, 174 million. He stresses that this is a stress calculation, not a claim that the line is fully shut.

2. The rebuild now runs to 2033–2036

In his previous paper Miller set a five-year horizon for rebuilding the damaged Gulf energy complex. He has now extended it to seven to ten years for the most severely damaged, interconnected systems, meaning recovery between roughly October 2033 and October 2036. Partial output will return sooner, but full, reliable operation will not.

The reason is equipment. Large compressors, turbines, high-voltage transformers, specialized pressure vessels and integrated control systems are custom-built and cannot be pulled from a warehouse. His critical path for replacing such a package is 84 months: a year to define the damage and fund the design, three years to procure and manufacture, two years to deliver and install, and a year to commission and stabilize. Insecure sites, financing gaps, factory queues and repeated attacks could add up to three more years. As he puts it, money can reserve a manufacturing slot, but it cannot compress every stage of engineering and fabrication.

3. A bill of $550 billion to $2.28 trillion

Miller models the reconstruction of the wider Gulf energy system, Saudi Arabia included, in three scenarios. He is explicit that these are funding envelopes built on stated assumptions, not audited damage estimates and not a Saudi-only bill.

Controlled Central Severe
Base reconstruction capital $400 bn $800 bn $1,400 bn
Execution uplift (security, delays, escalation) $100 bn $280 bn $630 bn
Finance and startup liquidity $50 bn $120 bn $250 bn
Total funding envelope $550 bn $1.20 trn $2.28 trn

Source: Karl W. Miller, Saudi Arabia: The Breaking Point (12 October 2026). Covers the broader Gulf reconstruction portfolio.

In the central case, $180 billion must be committed in the first two years alone, rising to $540 billion in years three to five. Over seven years that averages more than $170 billion a year. And every Gulf state will be competing for the same manufacturers, engineering firms, fabrication yards and specialist crews. A transformer slot taken by Kuwait or Qatar is one that Saudi Arabia does not get.

4. Delay is expensive

Miller puts numbers on what waiting costs. A three-year delay on the central program could add $76 billion to $125 billion in cost escalation and another $42 billion to $90 billion in financing charges. Meanwhile the fuel must still be bought somewhere: each year that 1 million barrels a day of fuel supply stays offline means 365 million barrels to replace, about $55 billion at his illustrative price of $150 a barrel. Leaving his full 3 million barrel-a-day gap unrepaired for three more years implies nearly $500 billion in replacement purchases.

5. The diesel gap gets wider

Miller's baseline remains a minimum global shortfall of 3 million barrels a day of diesel and jet fuel. The Saudi attacks threaten to push it higher. If disruption leaves 1 million barrels a day of crude unable to reach working refineries, the loss of diesel and jet fuel is roughly 300,000 to 450,000 barrels a day. An additional net loss of 500,000 barrels a day would raise his baseline to 3.5 million, an increase of one-sixth, adding 15 million barrels of shortfall every month.

He is careful not to double count: lost crude, the refinery output it would have produced and the missed export cargo may all be the same barrels. But the direction is clear. Saudi Arabia was the Gulf's main source of relief. If its bypass is unreliable, the global deficit grows.

6. America cannot fill the hole

Miller's test of American capacity is sobering. Over the four weeks to October 2, US refineries produced about 5.17 million barrels a day of distillate, exported 1.56 million and used 3.77 million at home. Replacing a 3 million barrel-a-day gap from the United States alone would require 58% more distillate output than American refineries produce today. US production is only about 150,000 barrels a day higher than a year ago; the global gap is nearly 20 times that. Promising more exports does not create more fuel. It simply moves the shortage from one buyer to another and drains American inventories.

7. Food, freight and flights

The fuel crisis is already reaching the real economy. Cereal prices are 17.2% higher than a year ago. Farmers need diesel before the harvest pays, truckers before their invoices are settled, and refrigeration before food reaches the shelf. Airlines need certified jet fuel at the airports they serve, and diesel cannot substitute for it. Miller's warning is that the weakest buyers, countries short of foreign exchange and credit, will not just pay more. They will be priced out entirely.

My take

Miller's assessment confirms what I have been arguing for months: the energy damage from this war is not a temporary price spike that ends when a ceasefire is signed. Reopening a shipping lane does not rebuild a refinery. Saudi Arabia, which only months ago was the world's insurance policy, is now itself a source of risk, and its economy shows it: Saudi oil activity fell by a quarter in the second quarter and GDP shrank 4.8%. The rebuilding of the Gulf will be measured in years and trillions of dollars, and the world will be short of diesel for much of that time.

That should be the frame for every promise coming out of Washington, whether it is Russian diesel, export bans or claims that prices are about to fall. As Miller concludes, recovery will be proven by fuel actually delivered, not by repairs announced or by a lower headline price.

title: Putin Proposes Summit With Trump And Xi To Negotiate End Of Ukraine War; Zelensky Not Invited
desc:
Putin Proposes Summit With Trump And Xi To Negotiate End Of Ukraine War; Zelensky Not Invited

Amid an escalating war that appears to get farther from any hope of a ceasefire, let alone peace, late on Sunday the WSJ reported that Vladimir Putin has proposed that he, President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet next month to talk about Ukraine in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year conflict that would favor Moscow.

Citing people familiar with the discussions, the WSJ notes that the plan represents an effort by Putin to capitalize on warming ties between Trump and the Russian leader that have alarmed Ukraine and its allies in Washington and Europe. Such a summit - one notably without the involvement of Zelensky who appears to have terminally alienated Trump in recent days - would be "unprecedented and send alarm bells ringing in European capitals and beyond."

According to a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter, Putin floated the idea in an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump. That conversation also produced a deal for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale on the global market. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions were taking place over a potential meeting.

“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told The Wall Street Journal.

A senior US official said that while Trump hadn’t agreed to such a summit, he said that the president could be receptive to the idea, given his desire to fulfill a campaign promise to settle the war. Trump had said it would be finished on “day one” of his new term, but he is now approaching nearly two years in office.

The Kremlin has suggested holding the trilateral dialogue on the sidelines of the coming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, the people familiar with discussions said. That gathering takes place on Nov. 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, the southern Chinese tech hub.

A potential three-way dialogue on Chinese soil would mark a big step for Xi in his efforts to elevate China’s role as a diplomatic power broker, said analysts who study China. Russian officials proposed the idea to Beijing through diplomatic channels and the Chinese side has indicated it wouldn’t object if Trump is on board.

“China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the U.S. and Russia,” said Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center, a Washington think tank.

While Putin had unsuccessfully proposed a trilateral summit to both Trump and Xi on previous occasions, this time, however, it comes during a reversal of Moscow’s fortunes with Washington.

Trump just notched a deal with Putin to get Russian diesel in a bid to lower fuel prices that have slowed the American economy and hurt Republican prospects ahead of the midterm elections. On Friday, Trump halted implementation of sanctions that were to be imposed on Russia under a bipartisan bill he signed last month, drawing criticism from lawmakers, including some of his allies.

The senior White House official said Trump made the decisions after seeing few other good options to lower prices.

At a time when Diesel prices are soaring, in part due to limited Russian exports amid a constant drone campaign waged by Ukraine against its refineries, Trump has shown renewed frustration with Zelensky, saying the Ukrainian leader must stop strikes on Russian refineries and suggesting that the country needs a new president. U.S.-led efforts to broker an end to the war, meanwhile, have been largely stalled.

In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump took aim at Zelensky, following Ukraine’s strike on an oil terminal in Putin’s hometown of St. Petersburg earlier in the day. He accused the Ukrainian leader of targeting Russian diesel refineries and said he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.” The president said he was holding off on imposing sanctions because he didn’t want to drive Russia away from the bargaining table. “I WANT THIS WAR END!” he wrote.

According to the WSJ, Moscow sees a potential trilateral dialogue as a way of cementing Russia’s membership in a club of great global powers, a status Putin has sought since he entered the Kremlin in 2000. The format also excludes from the picture Europe, which the Kremlin sees as its main obstacle to clinching victory in Ukraine.

The former Russian intelligence officer who was the WSJ source, said Putin has broad, if unrealistic, ambitions for the trilateral format as a second Yalta summit, which would divide up the globe into spheres of influence.

Even if Xi and Trump are unlikely to agree to that, the image of the American, Russian and Chinese leaders negotiating the fate of one nation would be a powerful signal. In Taipei, it could reinforce fears that Taiwan’s own future might be one day bargained over in a similar forum, particularly as Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring the self-governing democratic island under its control.

That said, a summit isn’t without risk for Xi. Chinese officials have concerns about allowing a geopolitical side show to overshadow their designs to use APEC as a showcase of China’s role in the region, said some of the people close to the discussions.

Xi is attempting to walk a fine line between continuing his support for Putin and maintaining China’s economic ties with Europe, the people said. A trilateral meeting like this could risk drawing China more directly into the Ukraine conflict and provoke a backlash from European capitals already wary of Beijing’s tilt toward Moscow. Although, with most European capitals desperate to either export or import from China, it isn't clear what if anything that can do to express their "outrage."

title: If This Was A Normal Week...
desc:
If This Was A Normal Week...

Submitted by Peter Tchir of Academy Securities

Maybe it was because I was in Europe that last week didn’t seem “normal.” Maybe that is why some of the things that I would think are most topical don’t seem topical (or at least weren’t what markets were responding to?). Or maybe it was just a weird week, where the underlying narrative wasn’t as much about the usual suspects, and was much more about supply (of bonds, energy, chips), stop losses (in every market everywhere), and dismal depth of true liquidity (or what we refer to as faux liquidity?).

In any case, much of the price action fits well into our recent narratives, and we were lucky enough to get to focus on yields not being driven by traditional data, and the warning signs coming from credit markets bright and early on Friday morning to kick off Morning Call on CNBC (which timewise wasn’t so bad from a hotel room in Paris).

Did Politics Even Matter?

There seemed to be no shortage of news on the domestic political front that individually might have moved markets, and collectively should have (and maybe it did play a role, but it certainly wasn’t the driving issue, which likely means it is lurking, making any recovery for risk takers more difficult):

  • Russian diesel. On September 18th the President signed the “bipartisan” Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. On October 17th (less than one month after signing the law and two days before the implementation deadline), the President waived part of the bill. Clearly a lot going on with the ongoing fighting with Iran, with the Houthis and Saudis fighting, and Russia and Ukraine continuing to attack each other, but again, a rather quick change to something that was actually passed through Congress.
    • Starlink managed to get itself dragged into Russia and Ukraine in a different way. Not only has Musk joined the President’s social media campaign that Zelensky must go (could just be a negotiating ploy, but it is out there), but there are also numerous reports that Starlink wasn’t working properly for the Ukrainian military. The reporting could be incorrect, and it may not have hit the valuations of any of Musk’s companies. Having said that, this, along with threats on restricting diesel exports, seemed to convince Europe that their dependence on the U.S. is quite fragile – which, for better or worse, is very good for ProSec™ going global.
  • The President put out a Truth Social post on October 14th on oil and Greenland. “Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland! There are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World…” The oil complex barely moved on this post. The market seemed to instantly “fact check” the word “our” as well as “easily available.” It seems like only a few weeks ago an announcement as bold as this would have moved markets, at least for a little while? Maybe all of the algos, especially any that paid for early access (according to Grok the program was implemented though it is unclear how many, if any, signed up), have lost so much money trading on Truth Social posts that they’ve been given time-outs by their controllers? News agencies are still reporting things like this as “Breaking News,” but markets have become far more discerning, which is an interesting development as volatility has increased of late.

While none of these themes seem to have directly induced any of this week’s market moves, I find it difficult to believe they aren’t playing any role.

We are in the midst of a changing world order, with multiple hot wars in progress, so it seems extremely difficult to believe that things impacting the policy and credibility of the U.S. aren’t contributing to market moves.

Diesel

Last week we went into some detail on Diesel and Yields. We argued that:

The Russian Diesel Deal was too small to matter:

  • Markets seem to have agreed that the amount was small and whatever they could export they were going to export anyway. Also, the President “seemed” to back off the concept that the exports were coming to the U.S., expressing it more as a gift to the world.

The EU release of diesel was bigger and more important, and could disappoint:

  • The IEA and the EU seemed to have come in around the “middle of the road” in terms of their decision. From all accounts, the IEA and Europe have largely agreed to accelerate the remaining reserves that were agreed to be released back in March of this year. So, it isn’t 50 million new barrels. It is around 20 million barrels that will be released sooner than previously scheduled, assuming each government that has unfulfilled release “quotas” fulfills their part. That seemed far from certain last week because the calculus around the war between Russia and Ukraine has changed (at least for many Europeans).

Diesel Export Ban

  • I think that would be a mistake (more on what it does for future trade (not good) than for how it helps in the near term (marginal at best)). The admin backed off of that concept, but who knows in this “rapidly evolving” policy-making atmosphere.

Need Agreements in the Conflict Zones

  • Despite the shift in focus to Russia and Ukraine, the most immediate boost would come from a resolution in the Middle East. While oil is making it out of the region with some regularity, there is no evidence that there is as much success with distillates. After months of conflict, the region seems to be getting trickier, rather than easier to assess from a military or diplomatic standpoint, but it is the key to getting all fuel prices significantly lower.
    • The U.S. blockade on Iranian shipping is clearly working. Presumably, greater enforcement of sanctions is also working, but that is more difficult to ascertain. This is good for putting pressure on Iran, but not great for energy prices. I’m in agreement that it is probably a small price to pay to try to change the policies of Iran. It will turn out to be an incredibly cheap price to pay if it succeeds in doing that.
    • Both the Houthis and Iran seem to be willing and able to hit targets, causing the entire region to remain on precarious footing. To the extent they are curtailing supplies it is bad for prices with no benefits accruing to the U.S. (unlike the U.S. blockade).
    • The countries within the region seem to be rapidly reassessing what stance they want to take with the U.S. (evidence of distancing), with Israel (mixed, but in some cases more cooperation), and with Iran and the Houthis/Saudi Arabia (so far seems to be leaning towards some expedient way to “get back to normal” rather than broadening the conflict, with the exception of the Houthis/Saudi Arabia conflict).
  • Back to Russia and Ukraine.
    • As of now it seems like it is up to Europe and Ukraine itself to figure out how to continue to prosecute the defense. Presumably there remains significant support behind the scenes from the U.S. (though difficult to tell at the moment), but going forward it seems clear that Europe and Ukraine had better figure out if they can do this alone (it seems like they are getting comfortable that they can).
    • Ukraine agreed to hold off on attacking Russian refineries and did so for a couple of days, but resumed when Russia did not reciprocate. Do we get another attempt at such a ceasefire where this time Russia obliges? It is quite possible, but it is only going to have a second-order effect on energy prices globally (not bad, but only okay, not game-changing).
    • Putin can do what he wants. Zelensky is restricted by a constitution. Iran may have no viable leadership with which to negotiate. Maybe that is why it appears that the President has gravitated to working more closely with Russia as they are the only ones in position to do something decisively (and in a way that might maximize the benefit to America)?

Not optimistic on a big decline in energy prices anytime soon, but it cannot be ruled out, so be careful being too bullish on the commodities themselves. Owning energy producers, globally, is still my main focus, knowing that there will be a sell-off (hopefully small and brief) after any resolution, because longer-term energy independence is the order of the decade.

Apologizing For A Record Number of “Seems”

Using the word “seems” is weak. Period. End of story. It is a cop-out. And yet, try as I might, I cannot gather the courage to eliminate “seems” and be more assertive in this report. There are two main reasons:

  1. I am reasonably certain that whoever speaks to the President last has the best possible available information at the time. The recency effect is in full swing. If you talk to the President at 8:30 am you have the best information available to anyone. But, by 3:30 pm, whoever speaks to him then has the best information, which may or may not have changed, with or without a catalyst to change it. This ties directly to some points I was trying to make in the first section.
  2. It is incredibly unclear what is a change in policy or what is just a negotiating point that was never meant to be policy. It is perfectly rational with so many things going on that the admin has to keep its real agenda very secret. Telling everyone exactly what we are planning is unlikely to help our position. Yet, it is difficult to ascertain what is noise and what is signal when we are bombarded (figuratively, not literally) with information every single day.

So, while it is a cop-out to use “seems” so frequently, I cannot get comfortable being more assertive, when in the back of my mind, I know we could get messaging from the admin that completely contradicts one of the views I espouse.

Two things I can say with complete conviction:

  1. The world is moving to ProSec as we’ve passed the tipping point in the ability to bring global trust back to where it was.
  2. After the midterms, no matter what, we will be discussing the U.S. steps on ProSec™, though what is prioritized and how it is implemented may start to change.

For those not familiar with what started as National Production For National Security (and resilience), which we now refer to as ProSec (Production for Security), here are two of our longer reports on the subject:

  • ProSec 2026 and Vertically Integrated Nations from July 2026.
  • ProSec 2026 from January 2026.

Now that we are moving on to markets, where I feel on more solid ground (despite the volatility), we can try to reduce the use of “seems.”

Yields, Spreads, Signals, and Liquidity

Two weeks ago, for the first time in a long time, we focused on not just Treasury Yields, but also Credit Risk in Something is Rotten in the State of Yields. Last weekend we argued that enough had occurred that both the bulls and bears could take some heart from the price action. This week, definitively on credit, we moved from a yellow alert to an orange alert.

We will not rehash the work from two weeks ago (this report is already getting long, and much of what we argued then, remains the case today).

We will highlight a few things and emphasize a couple of others that really bear more attention:

  • The size and speed of moves.
    • The move from 4.4% to 5.35% in three months in the 10-year Treasury was noticeable. It was a bit more of a steady grind, but during that entire move, there were barely any pullbacks. This week’s move of 17 bps was quite sizeable and rapid. The size and speed work in both directions. I believe the biggest driver of lower 10-year yields this week was the anticipation/hope/maybe even fear that the “compute”-related debt issuance might be set to be slower than anticipated. Economic data? Nah. The Fed? Nah. The deficit? Nah. Positioning and some respite from corporate issuance? Heck yeah.
    • European Sovereign Credit Risk. German vs French (and Italian) 2-year bonds blew out 50 bps in 2 days. That fits our definition of size and speed. Was there some news that drove that move? “Drove” is too strong of a word. Catalyzed a view around issues that had been hanging out near the hoop, but hadn’t yet caused a reaction? It is more plausible that the narrative, once expressed, tested liquidity (too little) and positioning (too complacent).
    • You can now add at least some of the “compute” issuers to that size and speed risk. We will come back to credit in a moment, because my biggest fear has little to do with actual credit risk and everything to do with size, positioning, and a false risk management comfort in liquidity.
  • Volatility – MOVE vs the VIX
    • In “Something Rotten” we highlighted that the VIX was well below its average for the year while the MOVE index was almost at the peak it hit in March. VIX finally moved on Thursday and especially on Friday, but still closed well below levels it hit as recently as in June and July and well below 30, which it breached during the early days of the Iran conflict. VIX is relatively useless as a predictor since so many “income alternatives” serve to suppress vol.
      • Selling volatility, in many shapes and forms, has become an “income alternative” for many individuals, wealth managers, and institutions. (I think we can safely say that vol selling strategies are one reason the “traditional” 60/40 strategies are not investing anywhere close to 40% in bonds for their income). As an overall theme, just as we are getting more bond supply from governments and corporations, asset managers are reducing their allocation on a percentage basis. There is an almost cult following (a very smart cult to be sure) of the JEPQ and JEPI roll dates ($90 billion of combined ETF AUM). Grok provided a quick list of other “vol-selling” equity ETFs, including QQQI, SPYI, QYLD, DIVO, GPIQ, and GPIX, that approach another $100 billion of combined AUM.
      • Will these vol suppression strategies continue to be able to suppress vol, or will they be forced to cover via outflows? Or for risk management? For now, I view these types of strategies as having suppressed equity vol, making things like VIX useless as a predictive measure, but they may also be the seeds of a much bigger move higher.
  • Credit Beta vs Fair Value. That is probably an overly complex way of saying that I think the basis between where credit beta products are trading (CDX indices and Credit ETFs) and where their fair value plays a major role in whether moves will be contained or they risk accelerations.
    • The good news is that HYG, JNK, LQD, VCSH, and JAAA as a sample of the high yield, long-dated IG, short-dated IG, and AAA CLO sectors are all trading right around their NAV. JBBB (BBB CLO) and ANGL (fallen angel) are trading at a slight discount, but nothing to get too worried about as signals from these aren’t as reliable as those from some of the other ETFs listed.
    • The CDX index is trading slightly tighter than its intrinsic value (according to Bloomberg), which is actually positive for my theory as the “arbs” would be selling protection on single names and buying protection on the index, which tends not to reinforce moves to wider and wider spreads. That being said, I’m not sure how accurate the “intrinsic” value calculation I’m seeing on Bloomberg is. Let’s call this “jury is still out.”
    • So far, even with the spread widening we have seen, it has been orderly, in terms of the underlying bonds and the beta products. I would fade that “orderly,” as I suspect we are moving into the fast and furious stage.
  • Two-week-old new issues. I think the liquidity in new issues that are a week or two old is very important to observe. I’m not arguing that they have to be trading better than their new-issue spread. Markets move. What I’m looking for is if you can pick up the phone and sell a block of $25 million on the wire. In “good” times, those bonds that are 1 to 2 weeks old are still fresh enough for dealers to support. Still new enough that the index crowd should be buying them or looking to buy them into month-end. They also tend to be the bonds that people use to manage risk in the early stages of de-risking (you don’t want to be seen as flipping new issues necessarily, but you can justify “lightening” up on some of those types of bonds). Probably the biggest thing I missed this week from being on the road is a good sense of where the “day-old bread” equivalents of new issues are trading. Lots of dealers making live 2-way prices, or having to pick and choose who you engage with as a seller to get the best execution? From our trading desk, which has been growing in volume, where Paul Giroux continues to expand Academy’s presence in secondary trading, the sense is that dealers are pulling back with liquidity and being cautious. Another reason to fade the idea that “orderly” will continue.

I’m as nervous and cautious on corporate credit risk as I’ve been in a long time. It has little to do with credit quality and everything to do with positioning and a false sense of liquidity that has not yet been tested. But, judging by what we’ve seen in credit-adjacent markets (fancy way of saying France, Spain, and Italy), any test could get ugly quickly (yes, I will use “ugly” as a legitimate term). But let’s call that 10 to 20 bps on IG and 3 to 5 points on HY.

I believe that the risk to a large fast move to the downside is much greater than the chance that we see a big move tighter.

Equities

Virtually everything written about credit and rates applies to equities. The positioning, vol suppression, and faux liquidity apply as much to equities as to credit.

Furthermore, it doesn’t surprise me that equities held up to rising Treasury yields quite well. It would surprise me if equities stand up to rising credit spreads as well, especially when the spreads are hitting the sectors that are driving equity returns and the economy – compute spend/build!

Given my view on the risk/reward on credit, I have to be very cautious on the equity side of things.

I will add one issue that I think is not only “unique” to equities, but is also a driver of equity returns that doesn’t get enough attention (though the T-Report does mention it frequently) and that is the “mechanical” buying and selling, not just of top-heavy indices (indices where a handful of names dominates the index on a percentage basis) but also the leveraged ETFs. Of particular concern is that the Nasdaq 100 and the SOXX Semiconductor indices have both top-heavy weighting, and a large amount (in number and volume) of leveraged ETFs, including on single names.

  • Focusing solely on leveraged ETFs (ignoring the top-heavy nature of the indices themselves), the Nasdaq 100 (according to Grok) has TQQQ, QLD, and SQQQ, adding up to close to $60 billion.
    • From a positioning standpoint TQQQ (3x Nasdaq 100) has a $34 billion market cap versus SQQQ (-3x Nasdaq 100), which has a $2.2 billion market cap. This would indicate positioning is aggressively bullish. SQQQ has had some inflow, but it looked like there was a lot of “profit taking” or more likely “just get me out of this” on Friday. TQQQ had some selling starting in mid-September, but the dip buying began in earnest. Retail dip buying has been smart, but at almost its largest AUM, how much more can go into it?
  • For SOXX, SOXL is the juggernaut at $22 billion, with things like SOX and USD adding another $5 billion or so.
  • On the single-name side of things, most are small, but with NVDL leading the way, there is probably $4 billion tied up in leveraged ETFs on NVDA. MUU is roughly that size. While others haven’t gained the traction, there is a lot of speculation and potentially “mechanical” buying in this sector.

Finally, there was a lot of speculation around another fund getting into trouble (and I did follow some accounts that claim to follow Leopold’s trading (if you know, you know)), but it would be too simple if this recent high and recent low follow the same pattern as Situational Awareness. It is possible, but I doubt it. Check out August’s piece on Situational Unawareness.

A Strong View That Might Require Too Many Contortions

I have a very strong view on what could play out in the coming days (weeks). I think it is perfectly logical. Yet, it requires a couple of “leaps of faith” outside of the ordinary to work.

  • The sell-off in credit and equities starts with the compute space widening.
  • The compute equities do poorly because the spending and buildout are a key part of their valuation.
  • Other credit spreads start to widen, not because their own credit has changed, but positioning, losses in other names, and relative value demand it.
  • This is the tricky part. At some point investors start pricing in a slowdown for compute-related debt issuance.
    • Compute-related spreads tighten. (That isn’t the tricky part).
    • Compute equities, general credit spreads, and general equities all continue to sell off. This is the tricky part.
      • If wider compute spreads started the selling, wouldn’t tighter compute spreads end it or even reverse it?
      • I guess my case rests on the idea that once we’ve started triggering selling, even once compute bond spreads reverse, investors will be very nervous about the state of the overall economy. Compute spend was a big part of the overall spend. Compute valuations may sell off more, as reacting to widening spreads with lower equity is normal, but the real hit would take place if the growth potential for compute-related stocks gets downgraded as investors doubt the access to capital?

I deleted and re-inserted this section 3 times. It seems to be “too clever” and needs to rely on a few things happening that don’t happen that often in markets. Yet, it seems so plausible (yes, I did use that word again, but c’est la vie) to me, that I need to leave it in.

Bottom Line

Enjoy today, and I expect to see a lot of “green” dots on Bloomberg terminals tonight, despite how unreliable Sunday night trading sessions have been! The only thing more unreliable than Sunday night trading (which so often seems to reverse on Monday mornings) is the NFP jobs data, but we go through the motions on that one. At least tonight we can have the NFL on in the background or the MLB (while the Jays couldn’t make it back this year, at least the Dodgers are out), or I guess 60 Minutes if that is more your cup of tea!

A lot to digest and think about. Don’t hesitate to reach out to your Academy rep if you have any questions, thoughts, or just want to point out all the things I got wrong – it is the nature of the beast in these types of confusing and stressful markets! Take care, good luck, and I’m really excited to be on Bloomberg TV at 8 am Monday morning; it seems impossible as I write this that there won’t be a lot to talk about one way or the other at that time.
