title: "Escape Valve" No More: San Francisco Moves To End School Choice Lottery
desc:
"Escape Valve" No More: San Francisco Moves To End School Choice Lottery

Authored by Lear Zhou via The Epoch Times,

The San Francisco Unified School District (SFUD) board passed a resolution on Oct. 13 to replace the current lottery-based admission policy with a neighborhood-based system for elementary schools.

Board members voted 5-2 to develop a policy under which every student would be assigned to a neighborhood school based on their home address, with a seat guaranteed even if applying late. Programs such as language immersion, K-8 schools, and special education remain open to citywide students to apply.

There were two options up for the vote: Option B and Option C.

Option B would guarantee a seat at a child's neighborhood school for families who apply on time. Families could also apply to any other SFUSD school with available space, preserving broader citywide choice.

Option C would guarantee a neighborhood-school seat even for families who apply late. But families could apply elsewhere only to designated citywide programs, such as language immersion, K-8 schools, and special education programs.

SFUSD Superintendent Maria Su recommended option C, while the parents' survey favored option B.

About 65 percent of families responding to the survey did not believe the district would fulfill promises made in option C, according to Su.

"Option C will actually not let the district off the hook. It will require the district to be very intentional with how we resource our schools; it puts the responsibility squarely on the district to make sure that every single neighborhood school is worth choosing," Su told the board at the Oct. 13 meeting, promising that the schools have "safe, academically rigorous, and stable staffing by trusted adults."

The new policy would take effect in October 2027, following the board's approval on April 13, 2027, and would apply to the 2028-29 school year.

"Any district that goes through this type of turnover is at least going to take five to 10 years," deputy superintendent John Davis told the board.

"There's going to need to be a lot of difficult discussions to get a strong staff at schools that have historically been disinvested in, through their community, through redlining, through all the negatives that our society has imposed on folks."

Under the current student assignment system, families can list any number of schools on their application in order of preference, and are assigned to their highest-ranked choice if seats are available.

If more students request the limited number of available seats at a particular school, a series of preferences is weighted in a lottery-like selection process to determine who gets the spot.

"It is every parent's responsibility to think about what's best for their kid. It is our responsibility to think about what's best for all the kids," SFUSD commissioner Matt Alexander said.

"The choice system creates an escape valve for the families that have the most wherewithal, the most understanding, the most ability to navigate the system and escape from schools that are perceived to be bad."

SFUSD commissioner Alida Fisher, who voted no on Option C, criticized the change. "Saying it will take time and yet forcing families into a system where we know we can't within two years equitably resource those schools and put the programs into place." she said.

"Frankly, we are screwing over families in certain parts of the city. Neighborhood schools will by definition be segregated schools."

The current student assignment policy, which applied from 2011, was initially designed to "reverse the trend of racial isolation and the concentration of underserved students in the same school," but the city's public schools became more segregated than 30 years before, according to SFUSD.

SFUSD commissioner Supryia Ray, who also voted against option C, said the elephant in the room is that SFUSD is facing a 14,000 enrollment gap.

"There seems to be some idea here that if we force people to go to their neighborhood school, outside of maybe citywide schools, somehow this will fill up all these schools," Ray said.

If the board chose option B, Su said, "Families who do not trust their neighborhood schools will continue to leave those schools; those schools will stay under-enrolled. And that pattern impacts our southeast neighborhoods the hardest."

Su argued that by choosing option C, the district could keep the funds in the southeast neighborhood and consider merging schools in neighborhoods with few students.

title: Tesla Wins Round In FSD False-Ad Suit As Court Tosses Class Certification
desc:
Tesla Wins Round In FSD False-Ad Suit As Court Tosses Class Certification

Authored by Matthew Vadum via The Epoch Times,

A federal appeals court blocked Tesla customers in California from pursuing class action claims that the company misled them about the hardware capabilities of its full self-driving (FSD) technology.

A class action is a lawsuit filed when a group of people or businesses suffer common injuries as a result of a party's alleged conduct.

For a consumer case to proceed as a class action, the buyers generally need to show they were all exposed to the same allegedly false statements in a similar way. Otherwise, each person's situation is too different for the claims to be tried together.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled on Oct. 16 that the case cannot move forward as a class action because every buyer's situation is different.

To sue collectively, the buyers would have to show that they were all exposed to the same allegedly misleading company-supplied information in essentially the same way.

The panel held that the plaintiffs could not show that every class member had seen Tesla's hardware claim - the company's assertion that its vehicles already had the hardware needed for full self-driving. The judges wrote that an assumption of exposure to the hardware statement makes sense with product labels, because "every purchaser necessarily has the allegedly misleading statement in front of him."

That was not true here, they said. As the district court recognized, "there [was] no specific requirement forcing [FSD purchasers] through the Autopilot page to complete their purchase," the judges said.

The upshot of the ruling is that thousands of customers that the lower court had certified as a class cannot, at least for the time being, sue together jointly in a single legal proceeding.

The ruling does not deal with the merits of the claim advanced by Thomas LoSavio and other California-based Tesla buyers that Tesla misrepresented the vehicles' FSD capabilities. They allege that the company's alleged deception led them to pay extra money for software they say doesn't work properly.

In August 2025, U.S. District Judge Rita Lin in San Francisco ruled that Tesla must face the class action.

She said the question of whether Tesla vehicles lacked sensors for autonomy, along with the company's inability to "demonstrate a long-distance autonomous drive with any of its vehicles," justified group lawsuits by two sets of drivers who purchased its FSD package.

Lin certified the plaintiffs as a class for the purposes of the litigation. She said thousands of individuals probably read the company's claim on its website from October 2016 to August 2024 that its cars were equipped with FSD, and that Tesla CEO Elon Musk made a similar claim at a press conference in 2016.

"While these channels alone may not ordinarily be enough to establish class-wide exposure for a traditional car manufacturer, Tesla's distinctive advertising strategy warrants a departure from the typical approach," the judge said.

Lin was referring to the company's direct-to-consumer model. Unlike traditional automakers that sell through dealers and lean on conventional advertising, Tesla directs most product information through its website and Musk's public statements.

The judge concluded that this made it more likely FSD buyers would have seen the hardware claim than would be true for a conventional car company.

The Ninth Circuit panel rejected that inference, finding Lin had improperly assumed classwide exposure. The panel vacated the class certifications and sent the case back to the district court for further proceedings.

Attorneys for the plaintiffs criticized the new ruling.

"We think the panel did not fully appreciate the unique circumstances here, and the importance of the hardware statement to Tesla's marketing campaign."

The Epoch Times reached out to Tesla for comment. No reply was received by publication time.

title: BTIG Spots "Real-World Evidence" Humanoid Robots Are Entering The Workforce
desc:
BTIG Spots "Real-World Evidence" Humanoid Robots Are Entering The Workforce

Goldman Sachs' recent upward revisions to global humanoid robot delivery forecasts through the end of the decade, along with rising estimates across Wall Street desks, point to broader expected adoption in factories, restaurants, and other workplaces. Military applications and household use could follow soon.

BTIG strategic opportunities analyst Jesse Sobelson told clients Friday that the physical AI boom is moving onto factory floors, into warehouses, and behind restaurant counters.

Sobelson and his team attended RoboStrategy's Robotics Founders Forum in New York this week and reported back on what executives from several of RoboStrategy's private-company holdings (Apptronik, Standard Bots, Dexmate, Maven Robotics, Path Robotics and Dyna Robotics) discussed: robot development, commercial deployments, and manufacturing plans.

"One of the central themes we took away from the presentations is that physical AI and robotics are moving beyond the "science project" phase and toward commercial utility," Sobelson said.

Sobelson said, "While AI-enabled robotics generates limited revenue today, every company we heard from presented solid evidence that real-world deployments are increasing, performance is improving rapidly, and the addressable market could expand significantly from where we are today. RoboStrategy presenters shared an analogy to early language models that we found instructive: LLMs initially suffered from hallucinations and weak contextual understanding but improved quickly as architectures, memory, data, and compute scaled. Some presenters contended that robotics appears to be following a similar trajectory, with some task-specific systems now completing tasks at greater than 99% accuracy."

He said Maven Robotics offered one of the clearest examples of the gradual rollout of humanoids but stopped short of saying a "ChatGPT moment" wasn't in the cards for the industry in the near term.

The following company-level takeaways reflect insights executives and insiders shared at the forum, which BTIG analysts attended.

Jeff Cardenas, CEO and Co-Founder of Apptronik

Apptronik stated it is pursuing a broad vision of humanoid robotics in which versatility, and not optimization around one fixed task, is the defining advantage. The company believes a single robot eventually needs to perform hundreds or thousands of tasks, allowing customers to shift the same asset between workflows as demand changes. The company argues this versatility is particularly compelling in the logistics vertical, where inbound and outbound activity can peak at different times of day and dedicated automation often produces unattractive utilization. Apptronik believes its modular approach separates mobility from manipulation, and that emphasizing two-armed manipulation is the most versatile architecture. In effect, the company explained that when it is attempting to put all these pieces together to build the “PC of robots”: a mass-manufacturable platform whose functionality expands through software and interchangeable configurations, rather than through consistently needed to re-deploy new hardware versions.

An immediate priority, according to Apptronik, is data and deployment. The company shared that Apptronik’s Robot Park is intended to function as a data factory, combining robot-generated data, egocentric human data and synthetic data to train and validate future systems. Customer programs with Mercedes-Benz (MBGYY, Not Rated) and GXO (GXO, Not Rated) were highlighted in the presentation as iterative learning processes, putting robots into real operating environments that should strengthen the deployment-data flywheel. The company believes collaboration with Google DeepMind is central to this strategy, linking foundation-model development with purpose-built hardware. Management also argued that its “show, not tell” posture reflects the depth of its engineering work (including more than 20 robot designs and roughly 80 actuator iterations) but the company acknowledges that Apollo 3 must ultimately demonstrate that these advances translate into manufacturability, reliability and useful out-of-the-box intelligence.

On deployment, management explained that they expect it to proceed in stages over time: warehouses and logistics first, followed by customer-facing settings such as healthcare and retail, and eventually homes and assistive care. This is because this sequencing appropriately prioritizes structured environments where the economics and workflows are easiest to prove. However, management argued longer-term urgency is due to demographic challenges: declining birth rates and shortages of caregivers could make assistive robotics a necessity rather than a convenience. Apptronik acknowledges the competition, and notes it is fighting to scale manufacturing and compress the transition from pilots to recurring commercial fleets before competing platforms establish their own data advantages.

David Golden and Leif Jentoft, Co-Founder and Head of AI Solutions at Standard Bots

In the conversation with Standard Bots, the company shared it is targeting what it sees as the largest practical barrier to industrial automation: it believes adoption has been limited because robots remain too difficult and expensive for most manufacturers to deploy. The company contends that adoption is concentrated among large automotive companies that can spend millions of dollars and months integrating a robot around a single repetitive process (such as the automotive industry). Outside those environments, Standard Bots believes penetration remains low because the integration burden overwhelms the potential return. The company argues its primary business proposition is to remove the “PhD” from deployment by allowing operators to configure robots through intuitive software (including conversational AI and an iPad-style interface) rather than specialized programming and custom engineering.

This focus makes deployment particularly urgent, according to the company. It has approximately 150 robots in service and is scaling operations in Ohio, while also operating a production facility in Glen Cove, New York. They believe the use of off-the-shelf hardware should reduce supply-chain risk and allow the company to concentrate investment on software, usability and application integration. Reliability nevertheless remains non-negotiable for the management team: they state an easy-to-program robot has limited value if downtime stops a customer’s entire production line. Standard Bots therefore stated its balancing rapid fleet growth with the need to establish industrial-grade dependability.

This led the company to explain its strategic advantage is less the robotic arm itself than the integration and data layers connecting the machine to the end application; deployments across small and mid-sized businesses may be especially valuable, according to the company, because they expose the platform to a broader variety of workflows than highly standardized automotive plants. It believes each customer installation contributes data that can improve models and product design, making the installed base increasingly difficult to replicate. The company's conclusion is that this creates a strong incentive to deploy now: the vendor that makes robotics accessible to bakers, machine shops and other non-expert users can build a differentiated data asset before humanoids or lower-cost foreign competitors broaden their reach.

Tao Chen, Co-Founder and CEO of Dexmate

Dexmate’s core argument is straightforward: a robot that can operate close to 24/7 can produce compelling economics even before fully general-purpose autonomy arrives. The company explained how it believes that seemingly small design choices (including camera positioning, actuator geometry and data infrastructure) can materially affect whether models can interpret the environment and transfer successfully into production, and that hardware with AI requirements incorporated from the outset rather than adding perception and intelligence to a legacy machine make for more efficient hardware. The company also explained that demand from frontier AI laboratories also provides technical validation and exposes Dexmate to advanced model-development workflows.

The discussion made it clear that it is not intent on winning the foundation-model race itself. Instead, the company wants to make existing AI models accessible and useful through integrated hardware and software. They see this as a pragmatic allocation of capital because model capabilities are advancing rapidly across the ecosystem, while installation, training, workflow adaptation and user experience remain persistent customer bottlenecks. Dexmate’s argued that its differentiation must therefore come from faster integration, easier operation and lower total cost rather than from claiming the most advanced proprietary model.

Manufacturing and logistics represent the most immediate deployment opportunities, according to Dexmate, because customers can quantify labor savings and utilization easily, while the company contends that hospitals and hotels may follow more slowly given their less structured environments and higher sensitivity to service interruptions. The company also noted that requirements also differ materially among large customers such as electronics manufacturers, and robot training is not yet universal across platforms or applications. Dexmate’s near-term imperative is to reduce the time between installation and productive utility; if that friction remains high, the company believes lower-priced Asian hardware could capture the market despite weaker software integration.

Hamza Derbas, Founder and CEO of Maven Robotics

We understand that Maven Robotics is building a vertically integrated industrial robotics system spanning hardware, software and AI. The company notes its initial focus is work that remains predominantly manual despite decades of factory automation: moving containers, handling totes, mixed-case palletizing and supplying production lines. It believes these workflows require more than a repetitive pick-and-place motion; robots must manage loose items, change tools, recover from anomalies and coordinate across long sequences. Maven shared its thinking on productization is that wheeled, dual-arm architecture and quick-change end effectors attempt to combine versatility with higher throughput than a fully generalized humanoid. The platform is reportedly capable of carrying roughly 30 kilograms and changing tools to open, manipulate and precisely stack different items.

Importantly, management does not claim that one model can perform every industrial task today. Maven instead explained it occupies a middle ground: progressing toward generalization while delivering economic value in defined workflows now. Its software reportedly reduces implementation from months of custom programming to a much shorter configuration process, and learning from one robot can propagate across the fleet. Acccording to the company this is critical because customer demand appears to exceed current supply. Maven reported it has five customers, including several that could eventually support fleets of thousands, and expects deployments across roughly 10 sites with multiple robots per sit, and management emphasized that these are intended as production contracts (not pilots or proofs of concept) which raises the urgency around manufacturing capacity and field reliability.

The company noted its capacity is currently modest at roughly 200–300 robots annually, but management outlined a modular factory model capable of producing approximately 2,500 robots per line, with an ambition to reach 25,000–30,000 deployed units in 2028. It contended that public market estimates broadly support an approximately $80–$100 billion opportunity for tote handling and palletizing, with broader assembly, fabrication and industrial-material-handling applications potentially adding several hundred billion dollars. The immediate constraint, in Maven's view, is therefore supply and execution, not market imagination: the company highlighted that customers facing labor shortages or existential pressure to automate want systems now, and any delay gives competitors time to capture deployments, operational data and recurring revenue. Elaborating on this shortage, Derbas noted that the Manufacturing Institute (MI) anticipates 4M job openings for manufacturing anticipated by 2030, with an anticipated 2.1M shortfall, and Deloitte worked with MI collaboratively to note an anticipated $1Tr in economic cost for shortfalls that need to be solved.

Scott Smith, VP of Finance at Path Robotics

Path Robotics notes it selected welding as its initial beachhead because it combines high labor cost, scarce skills and direct consequences for manufacturing throughput. The company found that welding is frequently a critical production bottleneck, and workforce availability is deteriorating; indeed, the American Welding Society estimates that roughly 320,500 new welders will be needed by 2029. Path believes its installed base of approximately 50 customers across multiple industries suggests that the value proposition is transferable, while successful economics in a relatively lower-cost manufacturing market such as Mexico would indicate even stronger potential in higher-wage regions.

The company believes its Robotics-as-a-Service model is central to accelerating adoption. Rather than requiring customers to justify a large upfront capital purchase and wait for a conventional payback period, Path aims to deliver operating-expense savings from the start and contract around annual productivity. This reduces the friction associated with automation budgets and shifts some performance risk from the customer to Path. The company deploys its own integrated hardware, with the company highlighting this is rather than relying exclusively on installed equipment, which it believes gives it greater control over performance but also creates capital, manufacturing and field-service requirements.

With welding economics established, Path postulated on expanding into the next logical steps: upstream assembly and fit-up (the work required to prepare components for welding). They believe that expansion could increase wallet share and allow Path to automate a larger portion of the production flow, while mobile platforms such as quadrupeds may extend welding into outdoor or difficult-to-access environments. Shipbuilding is a particularly compelling prospective market, according to the company, because welding intensity and constrained domestic capacity create an urgent need for productivity. The key execution risk that Path sees is if it can broaden applications without losing the high-return, repeatable deployment model that made welding an attractive initial use case.

Lindon Gao, CEO and Co-Founder of Dyna Robotics

Dyna Robotics is focused on dexterous, commercially useful workflows in laundromats, hotels, restaurants and gyms. Dyna stated these markets are attractive because textile and food-service tasks remain highly manual, repetitive and difficult for traditional automation. Dyna’s deployments include napkin folding for Din Tai Fung, where the customer is reportedly requesting additional robots, providing an important signal that the system can generate operational value rather than simply perform a controlled demonstration. The broader opportunity, according to Dyna, is to expand from an individual task (such as folding) to an end-to-end workflow covering handling, loading, unloading and sorting.

Dyna sees the principal gating factor for adoption being reliability. Gao believes customer acceptance in the 80%–90% range may be encouraging for an emerging system, but it is inadequate for unattended, scaled operation. Dyna’s goal of approximately 99.9% reliability is therefore not an incremental engineering target; it is the threshold between an assisted product and scalable automation. Extending demonstrations from one continuous hour (which Dyna has a posted video of) to 24 hours should expose the edge cases that matter in production, including dropped items, variable fabrics and the cumulative effect of small errors throughout a workflow. As management succinctly frames it, deployment itself is the most meaningful evaluation.

Dyna explained that its Taku hardware was developed internally to align the body, mobility and end effectors with these workflows. It believes a human-compatible form factor offers access to environments designed around people and benefits from abundant human task data, although that does not necessarily require a fully bipedal humanoid for every application. The urgency is clear, per Dyna's commentary: existing customers are asking for more systems, but scaling ahead of 99.9% end-to-end performance risks increasing support costs and damaging trust, in the company's view. Dyna states it must therefore expand deployments quickly enough to collect data while maintaining the balancing act of enough operational control to close the final reliability gap and maintain customer trust.

Circling back to Eric Sheridan, managing director and internet/e-commerce equity analyst at Goldman, he recently raised his base-case forecast for global humanoid robot shipments to 75,000 in 2026, 890,000 in 2030, and 6.5 million in 2035, versus previous estimates of 51,000, 256,000, and 1.4 million, respectively.

As we noted earlier this week, the rise of humanoid robots will further increase demand for advanced memory chips, which are already in short supply. However, some relief may be on the way as Chinese giant CXMT brings additional supply online next year.

title: Pimco Sees A 6% 10-Year... Here's Why "Bad Inflation" Caps Yields
desc:
Pimco Sees A 6% 10-Year... Here's Why "Bad Inflation" Caps Yields

Authored by Lance Roberts via RealInvestmentAdvice.com,

Will interest rates go up to 6%? That's the question on many investors' minds since Pimco's chief investment officer, Dan Ivascyn, told the Financial Times last Friday that a 6% 10-year Treasury yield is "certainly possible." This week's hotter-than-expected September CPI report only added fuel to that argument.

I get it. The 10-year closed at 5.31% on October 5, the highest close since May 2002. It started the year at 4.18%. However, look at what is actually driving inflation. Then look at how every major yield spike since 1990 ended. The case for a sustained move to 6% gets thin quickly.

Pimco's 6% Call, And Why It Landed

In case you didn't read the article, let's start with what Ivascyn actually said, because the headlines compressed it. He did not forecast 6%. He said it was possible, and he tied a big part of the recent move to market plumbing rather than economics.

"It is certainly possible, even from a short-term trading perspective... some of the activity we've seen in the last couple of weeks is tied to some negative technicals." - Dan Ivascyn, Pimco, to the Financial Times, October 9, 2026

Furthermore, he also flagged "stop-out activity from the platform hedge funds and other levered investors," and warned that a move to 5.5% or higher would bring "some decent weakness in risk markets, both credit and equity."

Read that last part twice, because I'll come back to it, and it was a topic we touched on when we discussed the "Basis Trade." The backdrop is real. Oil has spiked. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023. And today's CPI showed headline inflation accelerating to 3.7% from 3.4% in August.

Such is the setup that makes a 6% call feel inevitable. But a forecast that depends on forced selling by levered funds is a forecast about positioning, and positioning reverses. When the "technicals" that drove a move wash out, the fundamentals reassert themselves. So the real question for investors is what the fundamentals say.

Will Interest Rates Go Up On Inflation? Look Under The Hood

The bond bears' case rests on inflation. So let's look at inflation. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported this morning that the energy index rose 20.4% over the past year, with gasoline up 34.2%. Gasoline alone rose 9.1% in September. Strip out food and energy, and core CPI rose 2.6% over the year. A year ago, that same core rate was running at 3.0%.

Notice in the chart above that the red and black lines diverge in March 2026. That is the oil shock, and it hasn't spread into the core. Wages tell the same story. Average hourly earnings rose 3.0% over the past year, per the September jobs report, which is hardly a "wage-price spiral." Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, and July was revised to a loss of 10,000.

Is this the kind of inflation that sends yields to 6% and keeps them there? No. This is "bad inflation," the supply-shock variety that eats into household budgets until spending slows, hiring stalls, and the very price pressure that started the scare begins to fade on its own. It doesn't justify "higher for longer" forever. Gasoline now runs $4.33 a gallon nationally, up from $2.98 before the current oil shock (AAA data cited by CBS News). That extra $1.35 per gallon isn't spent elsewhere, and the economy slows under its weight. Energy-driven inflation without wage growth behind it is a tax on consumers, and taxes slow economies. Slowing economies don't sustain 6% bond yields.

Every Yield Peak Since 1990 Ended The Same Way

Bob Farrell's Rule #1 is that markets tend to return to the mean over time. Bond yields are no exception, and when I went back through the Federal Reserve's daily Treasury data and pulled every major 10-year yield peak since 1990, 6 of them stand out, and each one looked unstoppable at the time.

Here are the details of that research. The table below uses the daily closing high for each episode, then measures where the yield sat 12 and 24 months later. It also lists what was happening as yields fell, because yields rarely fall for "positive" reasons.

Step back for a moment and think about the data. Since 1990, there have been 6 interest rate peaks, and 6 periods of lower yields two years later. The mechanism was the same each time: higher rates tightened financial conditions until something gave, whether that was the economy, a levered corner of the market, or the Fed's resolve. The average decline was 1.64 percentage points, within a range of roughly 1 to 2.25 percentage points.

There are two caveats to mention. The first is that a peak is only a peak in hindsight. This study tells you how these episodes resolved, not the day they ended. Secondly, the 2018 figure includes the pandemic collapse in rates, which flatters it. Still, even 12 months out, every case was lower, by more than three-quarters of a point at minimum. So, will interest rates go up from here? They can, for a while. The history says that the higher yields climb, the faster they break the thing that is pushing them higher.

"Yields don't peak because investors get comfortable. They peak because something breaks, and at 5.3% the list of candidates is getting long."

Real Rates Are Already Doing The Fed's Work

This is where the data gets even more interesting. When we measure against core inflation, the 10-year Treasury now pays a "real yield" of roughly 2.7%. That's the highest since 2010, and well above the 1.6% average since 1990. Real yields are what borrowers actually feel, regardless of what the "soft landing" crowd says. A business deciding whether to build a plant is weighing that number, just as much as a family deciding whether to buy a house. This is why if you are wondering whether interest rates go up from here, you should watch "real yields" closely.

I've written about where I thought fair value sat for some time. To wit:

"By the mean-reversion logic the framework implies, the fair value of the 10-year is closer to 5.3% than to 4.6%." - Rising Interest Rates: Why The Narrative Fails Against The Data, May 22, 2026

Interest rates have already returned to normal, and a move to 6% would be an overshoot of roughly 70 basis points beyond fair value. That level would also arrive just as payroll growth has nearly stalled and unemployment has climbed to 4.2%.

"But Lance, the debt is far bigger now than in any of those past episodes."

I agree, and it certainly is. That is exactly why the overshoot is harder to sustain, not easier, because every extra point on the 10-year eventually rolls into the interest bill on the trillions of dollars of debt that Washington refinances every year. The CBO's preliminary numbers show net interest on the public debt hit $1.143 trillion in fiscal 2026. That's up 11% in a year and accounts for about 21% of all federal receipts.

Higher rates on a bigger debt pile drag on growth. That drag eventually shows up as lower yields, not higher ones. I made that case in detail in "Normal Interest Rates: What The Debt Panic Gets Wrong."

Will Interest Rates Go Up Further? What It Means For Investors

Go back to the line I asked you to remember. Ivascyn's own scenario says a move to 5.5% or higher brings "some decent weakness in risk markets, both credit and equity." That is precisely the environment in which high-quality bonds tend to do their job. If rates spike far enough to hurt stocks and credit, the spike itself often sets up the bond rally. In other words, the 6% scenario partly contains its own cure.

That doesn't mean loading up on long-duration bonds and walking away. In this past weekend's Bull Bear Report, we noted that we've slightly shortened clients' bond duration. Overall bond allocations remain in place. The trade-off is plain: duration protects you in a growth shock, when yields fall and bond prices rise, but it hurts you in an inflation shock, when yields keep climbing and longer bonds take the most pain.

If you are drawing income from your portfolio, a 5% yield is also a real cushion. It helps against the sequence of return risk I covered last week.

For the full case on owning Treasuries at these levels, see "Bonds At 5%: Is The 10-Year Treasury Finally A Buy?"

Waiting for 6% before doing anything is a bet in itself. Every peak in the table above looked like it had more room to run at the time. Whether interest rates go up another half point or roll over next month, a few basics hold. Know your portfolio's duration and whether it matches your time horizon. Staggering maturities means you're never forced to bet everything on one rate call. And if an oil-driven second wave would damage your plan, some inflation protection earns its keep. Such is the difference between managing risk and forecasting it.

Bottom line:The 10-year could touch 6% on forced selling, but with core inflation cooling and growth stalling, 6% looks far more like the top of this cycle than a new floor.

Every one of the last six yield peaks felt like the start of something new. Each one turned out to be the end of something old. The only question is what breaks first this time.

Authored by Jonathan Turley via JonathanTurley.org,

This election, Democrats have careened to the far left with calls to pack the Supreme Court, unleash a flurry of impeachments, and investigate Republicans. Few, however, have been as honest as Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D., Mich.) about the purpose of such threats. Slotkin recently said the quiet part out loud in an interview at my alma mater, the University of Chicago, admitting she wants to deter young people from even considering supporting the Administration... if they know what is good for them. Slotkin seemed to go full Col. Walter Kurtz in the middle of the interview.

The Chicago Thinker, an outstanding student newspaper at UChicago, posted an interview with Slotkin, in which she describes the strategy to deter young Republicans from getting involved in government, at least in supporting the Administration.

Like many of her Democratic colleagues, Slotkin is promising that, if Democrats are given back control of Congress, they will unleash a tsunami of investigations of Republicans supporting President Trump: In the clip of the exchange circulated on X, Slotkin states:

"I want to look at these signature cases and not just focus on the president, but on the people who enabled him. I want young people coming out of school to say, should I go work for the Trump administration? Like that sounds fun. I might get an opportunity. I want them to be like, Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want, and so let me avoid participating in that. I want that deterrence message."

"That deterrence message" is all too familiar to many Republicans. After January 6th, the Biden Administration used the riot to unleash a scorched-earth campaign against Trump supporters and groups.

ON UCHICAGO CAMPUS: U.S. Senator from Michigan Elissa Slotkin hopes planned political prosecutions of republican leaders will scare young conservatives from getting involved in politics. @ElissaSlotkin https://t.co/p7NBJpDcQW

— The Chicago Thinker (@ThinkerChicago) October 17, 2026

In an interview with CBS News, Justice Department official Michael Sherwin explained that they wanted to send a message with the harsh treatment of Trump supporters.

He explained that "our office wanted to ensure that there was shock and awe ... it worked because we saw through media posts that people were afraid to come back to D.C. because they're, like, 'If we go there, we're gonna get charged.' ... We wanted to take out those individuals that essentially were thumbing their noses at the public for what they did."

Of course, if Sherwin and his colleagues hoped to "Trump-proof" the nation, they failed in spectacular fashion.

However, that did not stop Jack Smith, who used his position as Special Counsel to seize the telephone records of Republican members of Congress while ordering carriers not to tell the members (some of whom were investigating Smith). We also learned recently that Smith collected information on over 600,000 Trump supporters and even tracked who bought MAGA hats.

Slotkin has been open about her desire to start a series of virtual show trials featuring Trump supporters to send a message to others. In a September 30 speech to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Slotkin compared the planned investigation to cleaning up Europe with what the Poles called "the Iron Broom": "The goal here is to have a list of signature cases that go after some of the most obvious and harmful abuses of taxpayer dollars."

To her audience's delight, she dangled possible 20-year sentences for figures ranging from the former CIA officer named Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to even U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro.

This appears to be a case of those abused becoming abusive figures. I criticized the Trump Administration for its investigation of Slotkin and five other Democrat lawmakers over a 90-second video urging military members to refuse illegal orders. While President Trump called the video "seditious" and "punishable by death," I viewed the video as clearly protected speech. In my book, The Indispensable Right: Free Speech in an Age of Rage, I argue for the elimination of sedition as a crime.

Now, Slotkin has surrendered any high ground that she had after the grand jury declined to return an indictment in February. The problem, it seems, is that simply the wrong people or party were targeted in such investigations.

The interview is evidence of the devolution of our politics where leaders are now fueling an anger addiction and promising unblinking rage in government. With many of her colleagues, Slotkin has gone full Kurtz.

In the film Apocalypse Now, Colonel Walter Kurtz (played by Marlon Brando) explained the secret to his success in suppressing insurgents. The key was to act "without passion, without judgment, because it is judgment that defeats us." In that way, he explained, he made "a friend of horror."

As Kurtz said, "Horror [now] has a face" and it is seen in the gallery of our politics of rage.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution."

Two Decades Of Mass Financial Delusion Ends Now
desc:
Two Decades Of Mass Financial Delusion Ends Now

Submitted by QTR's Fringe Finance

Friday’s selloff was not a surprise.

Between deteriorating credit markets, rising Treasury yields, increasingly absurd artificial intelligence valuations, enormous amounts of leverage and an entire financial system that has spent the better part of two decades mainlining cheap money like a frat guy guzzling Jaegermeister at the bottom of an ice luge, the warning signs have been flashing for quite some time.

The only real surprise, at least to me, is that it’s taken this long for equity investors to begin paying attention. And what worries me most isn’t how far stocks could fall, but how spectacularly unprepared investors are to deal with a market that actually goes down and stays down.

I want to start with something I read on CNBC this morning, because I think it perfectly encapsulates the extraordinary complacency and all around ignorance that exists on Wall Street. Discussing whether increased debt issuance could become a systemic problem, Michael Rosen, chief investment officer at Angeles, offered the following assessment:

“The question is: Is this a systemic issue? Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we’re not remotely close to that right now.”

I’m sorry. What? We’re not remotely close to excessive debt issuance?

The United States has more than $40 trillion in federal debt. Annual deficits are measured in trillions. Interest expense is approaching levels that would have been unthinkable a generation ago. Corporations are borrowing enormous amounts of money to finance everything from acquisitions and share repurchases to an artificial intelligence infrastructure boom whose eventual returns remain largely theoretical.

And that’s before we get to the trillions in private credit, leveraged loans, off-balance-sheet financing arrangements, GPU-backed borrowing and assorted financial engineering Wall Street has stuffed into every available corner of the economy.

But don’t worry, everybody. Apparently we’re not remotely close to excessiveness. Oh and don’t worry about the market going down…Jim Cramer blamed Friday’s sell off on a “big hedge fund blowing up”.

It’s hilarious to constantly be called a conspiracy theorist and then see the financial world’s predominant retail voice blaming a 2% move lower on “possible scenarios” about unnamed rogue margin clerks and hedge funds, before hoping to “start fresh” on Monday, as though $2 trillion in off balance sheet AI debt, dogshit private credit marks, positive real rates on the largest debt bubble in history and all the natural laws of mathematics are just going to go away if he closes his eyes and wishes hard enough for it.

If this isn’t excessive, what the fuck qualifies? Does the Treasury have to start issuing debt denominated in scientific notation? Do we need to start borrowing money to pay the interest on the money we borrowed to pay the interest on the money we borrowed?

Oh, wait.

The remarkable part isn’t the statement itself. Wall Street is a cesspool of delusion and ignorance like that. It’s that I suspect a significant percentage of Wall Street genuinely believes it. We’ve spent so long normalizing financial absurdity that the concept of excess has lost its meaning. And I think that complacency is going to make the next genuine market drawdown considerably more psychologically devastating than people realize.

As part of my award-winning1 “The World Is Ending, So Please Prioritize Renewing Your Paid Subscription To A Former Bartender’s Finance Substack” Series, on September 23, I published Bonds Are About To Crash The Stock Market, arguing that rising Treasury yields were threatening to expose the extraordinary amount of leverage and speculative valuation built into financial markets. As I wrote then:

“Rising rates are a slow, methodical wood chipper for anything built on cheap money.”

And we’ve spent the better part of twenty years building almost everything on cheap money.

My argument wasn’t complicated. When the risk-free rate rises, everything built on cheap financing becomes more difficult to justify. Equity valuations compress, refinancing costs increase, leveraged borrowers come under pressure and speculative investments requiring endless access to capital suddenly discover that capital has a price. The equity market can ignore that math for a while, invent new narratives and convince itself that artificial intelligence has somehow repealed the laws of finance. But it cannot ignore arithmetic indefinitely.

As I also wrote in that piece, the market has spent the last fifteen years assuming we would eventually return to the financial environment that followed the Global Financial Crisis: zero rates, endless liquidity, cheap leverage and central banks standing behind asset prices. Then I asked a question I think is becoming increasingly relevant:

“What if we don’t? What if this is the reckoning?”

There are legitimate reasons the market could find some relief in the near term. Lower oil prices, for example, could ease inflation expectations, reduce pressure on consumers and potentially give the bond market some breathing room after scorching producer prices rose the most in 4 years this past week:

And investors will keep looking to telegraph the Fed’s next move…as long as reading the tea leaves results in confirmation bias that rates are definitely going lower very soon.

Stocks found slight intraday relief for a few moments when, speaking in Bangkok during meetings of the International Monetary Fund, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to endorse or reject recent indications from colleagues that the central bank was in no hurry to raise interest rates. Warsh said he wouldn’t prejudge upcoming meetings, adding that the Fed was entering a new chapter in which it would no longer preview its decisions.

In other words, Warsh essentially told everybody that he wasn’t going to tell them anything. And the market managed to find some relief in that.

Which tells you something about the extraordinary degree to which investors have become conditioned to hang on every syllable uttered by central bankers. We’re now at the point where the chairman of the Federal Reserve declining to speculate about future policy decisions can be interpreted as comforting news.

For much of the recent turmoil, stocks and bonds have both been under pressure, consistent with fears about inflation, fiscal deterioration and higher interest rates. But Friday offered some evidence that the traditional flight from equities into Treasuries may finally be beginning to emerge. Longer-duration Treasuries rallied meaningfully, and the 30-year yield reportedly recorded its largest weekly decline since April 2025. That doesn’t establish a sustained rotation yet, but I think it’s something worth watching closely.

As equity losses accumulate, credit markets deteriorate and investors begin worrying less about inflation and more about preserving capital, I suspect demand for Treasuries could return in force. Yields could decline substantially even as equities continue falling. (Read: You Have To Like Bonds Here...Right?)

There is a world where falling yields are bullish for stocks because they reflect improving inflation expectations and a healthier economic outlook. And there is another world where falling yields are a symptom of investors becoming terrified of everything else. I think the second scenario deserves far more attention than it’s getting.

I suspect investors are going to be stunned if we enter an environment where Treasury yields fall, oil prices fall and equities continue getting their teeth kicked in anyway.

After years of conditioning investors to believe that lower interest rates automatically translate into higher stock prices, a genuine credit-driven bear market could be deeply confusing. If earnings expectations are collapsing, credit is tightening and investors are unwinding leverage, falling Treasury yields don’t necessarily rescue equities. They may simply indicate that the economy is deteriorating faster than policymakers can respond.

This is also why, as I wrote recently in You Have To Like Bonds Here...Right?, I’ve become increasingly interested in fixed income. Longer-duration Treasuries could benefit enormously from a serious economic contraction and eventual flight to safety. There are still risks, particularly if inflation remains stubborn or fiscal deterioration continues pushing yields higher, but I think the possibility of a reversal in rates is compelling.

And the truly fascinating possibility is that bonds could begin performing precisely when equity investors discover that the Fed can’t magically prevent every decline. (If they don’t, bonds keep crashing and gold heads toward $10,000 as the Fed implements yield curve control.)

One of the reasons I’m so concerned about what comes next is that, despite the selling we’ve already seen, I don’t believe we’ve come remotely close to clearing out the speculative excess built up during this cycle.

Take CoreWeave, which I’ve spent the last several days writing about. The company has become one of the poster children for the financial insanity surrounding the AI infrastructure buildout: enormous capital requirements, debt financing, GPU collateral, extraordinary growth expectations and a business model heavily dependent on continued access to capital. It should have never IPO’d if you ask me and if it wasn’t for Nvidia backstopping its IPO, it might not have.

As I wrote in my recent piece about Nvidia potentially being forced to support CoreWeave:

“They share an uncomfortable characteristic: the financial health of one participant increasingly depends on the continued financial health, spending and access to capital of everybody else.”

That’s a wonderful arrangement when asset prices are rising and a potential catastrophe when the music stops.

I suspect Nvidia may eventually find itself forced to intervene if CoreWeave’s financial condition continues deteriorating. Not necessarily because Jensen Huang wants to throw good money after bad, but because allowing one of the central financing mechanisms behind the AI boom to unravel could prove far more expensive than trying to save it. And even then, another investment might simply postpone the inevitable. (Read: Jensen Will Blink First)

CoreWeave is just one example, and frankly, it may be one of the more visible ones.

Look at crypto, where an enormous speculative ecosystem has developed around assets whose prices depend heavily on continued confidence, liquidity and risk appetite. There are legitimate technologies and businesses within that ecosystem, but also extraordinary amounts of leverage, financial engineering, questionable collateral and speculation.

What happens when investors discover that their crypto holdings, technology stocks and other speculative investments were effectively different versions of the same liquidity trade? And crypto doesn’t even need market forces to crash. It just needs…Democrats to win Congress in November: The Crypto Risk No One Is Discussing

Then there’s private credit, a market I’ve been warning about for quite some time. In this sector, the absence of daily price discovery is not the absence of risk. Sometimes it’s just the absence of a mirror: From Par To Pennies

Beyond that, there are leveraged loans, speculative real estate investments, private equity portfolios, venture capital valuations, structured financing arrangements and countless other corners of the market that have benefited from the same two-decade experiment in cheap money.

In my September 29 piece, It’s Official: The AI Emperor Has No Clothes, I wrote:

“Crises have a nasty habit of beginning from the ground up and working their way toward the assets everyone previously assumed were untouchable.”

I think that’s precisely the risk we’re facing now. And despite the recent selling, I suspect we’ve barely begun to uncover what’s hiding beneath the surface. The excess is still massive, the leverage is still massive, and the psychological complacency may be the most massive thing of all.

Here’s what I think people are really underestimating about the possibility of a major market drawdown: we have spent so long conditioning ourselves to believe that financial markets are supposed to go up that an actual sustained decline could produce a level of psychological hysteria unlike anything we’ve seen in decades.

I’m not talking about a garden-variety 5% correction or a couple of uncomfortable trading sessions followed by Nvidia announcing another $100 billion investment in somebody who will turn around and spend it buying Nvidia chips. I’m talking about a bear market where every rally gets sold, every supposedly cheap stock gets cheaper and every dip buyer who spent the last fifteen years congratulating himself for being a financial genius discovers that his entire investment strategy was predicated on the Federal Reserve making sure he never had to experience genuine discomfort.

I don’t think people have any idea what that would feel like anymore.

Why would they? For nearly twenty years, we’ve operated under a financial regime in which virtually every meaningful market disruption has eventually been met with lower interest rates, quantitative easing, emergency lending facilities, fiscal stimulus or outright intervention. We’ve trained investors to expect the rescue before they’ve even experienced the crisis. We’ve trained corporations to believe capital should always be available, private equity firms to believe valuations are whatever the last financing round says they are, and speculators to believe leverage is a permanent wealth creation strategy.

As I wrote in my recent piece about the potential return of boring blue-chip stocks:

“We’ve spent twenty years confusing asset price inflation with genuine prosperity, speculation with investing and central bank liquidity with actual wealth creation.”

We’ve spent two decades systematically eliminating financial discomfort, and in doing so, we’ve created a market populated by people who have almost no tolerance for it. That’s a hell of a psychological experiment, and I think we may be getting ready to find out what happens when it ends. (Read: Modern Chickenshit Monetary Theory)

The first genuine drawdown will be met with disbelief, followed by anger, accusations of manipulation, demands that the Federal Reserve do something and eventually, if the selling continues, people will be f*cking beside themselves.

And underneath all of that noise, the market will be doing something it hasn’t been allowed to do naturally for a very long time: attempting to price actual risk.

If that process really gets underway, I suspect the amount of financial garbage that gets exposed will be breathtaking. There are entire business models and sectors that have never been tested in a world where capital isn’t readily available.

Some of these assets will recover. Some will be acquired or restructured. And some will simply disappear. That’s what happens when financial markets begin distinguishing between businesses that create economic value and businesses that have survived primarily because the cost of capital was artificially suppressed.

And the process could be especially traumatic because we have an entire generation of investors who have been conditioned to regard every meaningful decline as temporary, every correction as a buying opportunity and every crisis as something that will eventually be resolved by somebody in Washington pushing a button.

We’ve become so accustomed to financial comfort that genuine price discovery could break our brains.

Of course, I could be wrong about the timing. Oil could retreat, Treasury yields could stabilize, the Fed could provide enough reassurance to spark another speculative rally and the whole circus could continue for another six months or longer. I’ve never claimed to know the precise date on which the market will finally lose its mind.

But I do believe the underlying excess is real, the financial vulnerabilities are enormous and the longer we postpone dealing with them, the more painful the eventual adjustment could become.

Imagine what happens when people discover there is no law of economics requiring their brokerage accounts, home equity, retirement portfolios or speculative investments to increase in value every year. I think it could genuinely break people’s brains.

And the irony is that none of this would be particularly extraordinary by historical standards. Financial markets have always experienced booms, busts, credit contractions, bankruptcies and periods of brutal repricing. What’s extraordinary is that we’ve spent the last twenty years convincing ourselves we’ve somehow evolved beyond them.

We haven’t. We’ve spent twenty years convincing ourselves that financial pain is optional. I think we’re getting dangerously close to discovering that it isn’t.

And when that realization finally sets in, I suspect the market crash itself may be the least remarkable part of the spectacle.

title: NRC Backs Fermi's Four Texas Reactors
desc:
NRC Backs Fermi's Four Texas Reactors

Fermi America's nuclear plans just cleared their first regulatory hurdle.

NRC staff have preliminarily recommended issuing combined licenses for four Westinghouse AP1000 reactors at Project Matador, Fermi's planned power and AI campus outside Amarillo, Texas, according to a draft environmental impact statement the agency put out for comment on October 9th.

Together, the four units would add over 4.4 GW of nuclear generation capacity to the private grid.

It took 15 months from application, and Fermi wrote the draft itself as the first test of an NRC pilot that lets applicants prepare their own environmental reviews under staff supervision. The agency expects that to cut its in-house review time by about half.

The NRC is targeting a final version in December. The harder part is the safety review, which has no schedule yet. Fermi pulled the site-specific portion of its application and plans to refile it by Dec. 31, and a mandatory hearing and Commission vote come after that.

Fermi wants its first reactor running by 2032, meaning the NRC is far from the company's problem.

Last November, we warned that storm clouds were gathering as Fermi struggled to sign its first major tenant. A month later, the stock cratered 50% when that prospect pulled out of a $150 million construction funding agreement.

In April, shares crashed another 22% after the board ousted co-founder and CEO Toby Neugebauer and the CFO resigned. As we put it then, "without tenants there is no company."

But, Fermi finally has one, on paper. In August, it signed a binding 15-year lease with TensorWave, an AMD-only GPU cloud, for 222 MW worth about $6.5 billion, with options to expand past 650 MW.

Phased delivery starts in the second half of 2027.

The lease hasn't closed yet. Fermi pushed the deadline from Sept. 30 to Oct. 31 to finish a lease guarantee, and it still needs project financing. On Tuesday, AMD agreed to provide credit support for the lease.

So AMD sells TensorWave its chips, has invested in TensorWave, and now backs TensorWave's lease. Circular?

Here it is: the latest, expanded AI circular financing chart https://t.co/a2RCRi4ygC

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 2, 2026

Still waiting on first power

On-site power is running behind. Last November, Fermi promised "1 GW of capacity online by late 2026." As of August, they moved the goal posts to "about 200 megawatts of initial commercial power over the next six months."

Fermi has taken delivery of six Siemens SGT-800s (nearly 300 MW) and three larger Siemens F-class units, and three GE Vernova 6B turbines reached the site recently. NAES has been hired to run the fleet, and Hillcore Energy Capital has signed a framework deal to finance, build and own about 2.6 GW more on site.

The old founder won't let go

Neugebauer, still Fermi's largest shareholder, sued over his firing in May.

He suspended a campaign to call a special meeting in July, and last month a Texas Business Court judge declined to temporarily block a 70% supermajority bylaw and new voting rules the board adopted after his ouster. He has since sued three directors.

The board, meanwhile, named former TerraPower CEO and Bechtel veteran Lee McIntire as CEO in August.

title: The Left's Rank Hypocrisy On 'Socialist Influencers'
desc:
The Left's Rank Hypocrisy On 'Socialist Influencers'

Authored by Thaddeus G. McCotter via American Greatness,

Far-left candidates court socialist influencers in primaries, then pivot to the center for the general election...

If memory serves me, while serving in Congress amidst a heated midterm battle in the mid-2000s, I made a cable television appearance where I was asked an "ambush" question. Well, it wasn't quite an ambush question, because the station in question was left-wing; hence, the anchor's Pavlovian parroting of the Democrat talking point du jour was really no surprise. The question was something along the lines of "Does every Republican blindly listen to Rush?"

"Who doesn't love a Canadian power rock trio?" I replied. My interrogator was nonplussed. I elaborated, "Though I do prefer Triumph."

In truth, the Rush in question was actually Mr. Limbaugh, who was at the height of his renown. Looking for an issue, the Democrats trotted out the canard that Republicans didn't work for their constituents but were in the thrall of a radio show host, following his dictates heedless of what the public wanted.

The Democrats' strategy quickly petered out, largely because Mr. Limbaugh's pro-American and commonsensical views were shared by scores of millions of Americans. Thus, even if some Republicans were influenced to one degree or another by Rush's views, those views were also shared by many of their right- and center-right constituents, who formed the base of their electoral coalition.

What evokes this memory is how the rank hypocrisy of today's leftists, particularly the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), regards their associations with social media, particularly radical leftist socialist influencers - one of whom, in fact, claims to aspire to being the radical version of Rush Limbaugh.*

The ideological difference between Mr. Limbaugh and today's shrill leftist socialist influencers is patent, as their anti-American content readily attests to their quest for clicks, celebrity, and money. (At present, I am unaware of these socialist influencers voluntarily putting their streaming revenues into a pool to be apportioned by a commissar for the common good of the oppressed.)

Be it hating all Americans or - as if to prove the depths of their animus - justifying the murderous terrorist attacks on our nation on September 11, 2001, or rationalizing away domestic left-wing political violence, these socialist influencers, to varying degrees of self-indulgent animus and self-imposed ignorance, aver that the "United States of Amerika" is irredeemably racist, misogynistic, inequitable, and wholly corrupt, and must be radically transformed into a socialist utopia by an omnipotent government controlled and commanded by them and their bilious, unproductive ilk, who have never run anything but their mouths.

Sane people would be tempted to think these anti-American, socialist cranks would be ignored by sound minds. They are. But sound minds are in ever-shortening supply these days. That is why they are increasingly being listened to and heeded by politically like-minded listeners.

In the instances of those listeners who become DSA and other ideologically aligned far-left candidates, there is the question of how truly they dance to the socialist influencers' tune - especially in electoral areas that are not deep blue progressive hellscapes.

What happens is the far-left candidate proclaims to the far-left, socialist, America-loathing voters how they, too, share that view. To help prove their bona fides as radicals and defeat a Democrat establishment candidate in a primary, they associate and, in some cases, physically appear with socialist influencers on the campaign trail.

Once they win their primary, however, the far-left/DSA Democrat realizes that America-loathing is not a great general election issue, so they begin to distance themselves not only from such socialist influencers but also from their own words.

One would hope such cynical duplicity would be readily identified so voters could factor it into their considerations. Unfortunately, we live in a world where the deceitfully named "accountability journalism" is a pandemic transmogrifying objective reporting into propaganda. As a result, when the far-left candidate is called on the carpet about embracing socialist influencers, the crucial bloc of independents views it, if at all, as just another partisan attack.

Consequently, the far-left/DSA candidate can casually dissemble how they are not there to disavow any social media influencer and how any past association with socialist influencers is a distraction by their GOP opponent, indeed a smear tactic. As they cynically race from the radical Left to the center in a general election, the far-left/DSA candidate hopes the voters miss the abject deceit in this defense.

The far-left/DSA candidate has actively embraced and aligned with the America-hating socialist influencer to court like-minded America-loathing socialists in his or her electoral coalition. Thus, while the far-left/DSA candidate claims not to have "disavowed" the socialist influencer, that is already known, because the fact is the far-left/DSA candidate has knowingly and cynically aligned with the socialist influencer and their listeners to win the primary.

Now, not wanting to lose these critical members of their electoral coalition, the far-left/DSA candidate gives a wink and a nod in the general election to keep their votes in his or her pocket without alienating independent and traditional Democrat voters. Meanwhile, this general election conversion from a far-left/DSA candidate into a center-left moderate is abetted by an ideologically sympathetic media that studiously ignores it.

One group that does not ignore it, however, is the socialist influencers. Throughout both their overt primary support and covert support in general elections, they have made no bones about how, once elected, the far-left/DSA candidate will answer to them - or else.

One can only imagine if Rush Limbaugh had made such claims against Republicans. Or, indeed, if Republicans had tried to win primaries by fist-bumping the far-right version of these socialist influencers and then scurrying to the center. They would rightly be pilloried by the press and the electorate.

People of good hearts know that hate is hate regardless of its partisan stripe and that it has no place in our American home. Yet, despite their lawn signs to the contrary, for the far-left/DSA candidates and their friends in a compliant press, not all haters are created equal, and their radical, socialist influencer haters, while muted for the moment as a matter of electoral necessity, are far from appeased.

If these radical socialist influencers get their way and their fellow-traveling far-left/DSA candidates get away with their cynical strategy and win, their America-loathing words will become deeds.

[*Author's note: I did not name the individual social influencers who disdain Americans and our country. I am not in the habit of giving these reprobates what they seek - name recognition, validation, and the clicks they crave that provide the revenue streams needed to propagate their anti-American screeds and promote their "careers." One rightly must support the freedom of speech. But no one is required to promote views they find repugnant. Feel free, however, to look them up and give them a listen, though I advise you to have the Alka-Seltzer handy.]

title: Here's Where Germany's 17 Million Immigrants Come From
desc:
Here's Where Germany's 17 Million Immigrants Come From

Germany is one of the world's largest destinations for international migrants, shaped by decades of labor migration, European mobility, and more recent refugee arrivals.

This graphic, via Visual Capitalist's Srijaa Chatterjee, uses UN international migrant stock data compiled by Our World in Data and analysis from DataPulse Research to show where Germany's foreign-born residents originated and where German-born emigrants live.

The figures represent people living outside their country of birth, rather than annual migration flows.

Where Germany's Immigrants Come From

The table below ranks the largest countries of origin for Germany's foreign-born population, based on data compiled by Our World in Data.

Rank Country of Origin Share (%)
1 🇵🇱 Poland 11.0
2 🇹🇷 Türkiye 9.0
3 🇺🇦 Ukraine 8.5
4 🇷🇺 Russia 6.8
5 🇷🇴 Romania 5.8
6 🇰🇿 Kazakhstan 5.4
7 🇸🇾 Syria 5.1
8 🇮🇹 Italy 2.6
9 🇦🇫 Afghanistan 2.1
10 🇨🇿 Czech Republic 2.1

Poland accounts for 11% of Germany's foreign-born population, followed by Türkiye at 9% and Ukraine at 8.5%. These populations reflect several migration waves, including postwar labor recruitment, EU labor mobility, and more recent humanitarian migration from Ukraine and Syria.

Germany's broader migration footprint extends beyond its foreign-born population. In 2025, 21.8 million residents, or 26.3% of the population, had an "immigration history," meaning they had immigrated themselves or both parents had immigrated. This measure also includes some people born in Germany, making it broader than the foreign-born population shown in the graphic.

Germany's Immigration Policies

Labor shortages have helped shape Germany's immigration policies. The expanded Skilled Immigration Act broadened pathways for qualified workers, including an Opportunity Card for job seekers and expanded access to the EU Blue Card. According to the OECD, reforms implemented in 2024 also made the recognition of foreign qualifications more flexible.

Alongside these labor migration measures, Germany has pursued integration programs and policies addressing asylum and irregular migration.

Where German-Born Emigrants Live

The U.S. hosts the largest population of German-born emigrants, at 1.1 million, or roughly one in four living abroad.

European countries also feature prominently.
